paragraphs: Bikila ran the Rome Olympic marathon without shoes not as a statement but because the pair issued to him did not fit comfortably and he feared they would raise blisters over 42 kilometres. He had trained barefoot for years in Ethiopia and simply trusted his own feet over new boots.

Running past torchlit ruins on a course that finished near the Arch of Constantine, Bikila pulled away from Morocco's Rhadi Ben Abdesselem in the final kilometres and won in 2 hours 15 minutes 16 seconds, a world best. No African had won Olympic gold before that day, and Bikila returned four years later in Tokyo to win again, this time wearing shoes.

Skateboarding, surfing and sport climbing were all contested at an Olympics for the first time at the Tokyo Games, held in the summer of 2021 after a year's pandemic delay. Skateboarding split into street and park courses; surfing ran off Tsurigasaki Beach depending on the swell; climbing combined speed, bouldering and lead into a single medal.

Japan's own Momiji Nishiya won the inaugural women's street skateboarding gold at 13, one of the youngest Olympic champions in any sport. The additions were part of a deliberate push by organisers to draw a younger television audience, alongside 3x3 basketball and BMX freestyle at the same Games.

Lamar Hunt tried and failed to buy an NFL franchise for Dallas before deciding to build a rival league instead. He recruited seven other wealthy owners, several likewise spurned by the NFL, and the American Football League was announced in 1959 with teams from Dallas to Boston to Denver.

The AFL began play in 1960 and survived a decade of financial strain by signing college stars the NFL wanted and by pioneering televised deals and two-point conversions. The rivalry forced a 1966 merger agreement, and the leagues' champions met in what became the Super Bowl, with a full merger completed in 1970.

The AFL and NFL had agreed to merge back in 1966, four years before it actually took effect, once a bidding war for college talent and the AFL's television deal made continued rivalry too costly for either side. The interim years produced the first two Super Bowls as a title game between the still-separate leagues, both won comfortably by the NFL's Green Bay Packers.

By 1970 the merger was complete: 26 teams split into the American and National Football Conferences, with some NFL clubs, including Baltimore, Cleveland and Pittsburgh, moved into the AFC to even out the numbers. The single-league, two-conference structure created that year has defined the NFL's organisation ever since.

Chad Rowan grew up in Hawaii and moved to Japan in 1988 to train in sumo under the ring name Akebono, entering a sport whose top rank, yokozuna, had never been held by anyone born outside the country. Promotion to yokozuna requires winning two consecutive top-division tournaments and approval from the Japan Sumo Association's judging council, not just results on paper.

Akebono won back-to-back tournaments in late 1992 and early 1993 and was promoted to yokozuna in January 1993, becoming the first foreign-born wrestler to reach sumo's highest rank. He held the title until his retirement in 2001 and was followed by other Hawaiian-born yokozuna, Musashimaru among them, before Mongolian wrestlers came to dominate the rank in the 2000s.

Vasily Alekseyev, a Soviet mining engineer turned super-heavyweight lifter, pushed his combined press, snatch and clean and jerk past 600 kilograms in 1970, a figure the sport's officials had treated as a natural ceiling only a few years earlier. He weighed well over 150 kilograms himself, and his bulk became as much a part of his reputation as the numbers he lifted.

Alekseyev went on to break roughly 80 world records over his career and won Olympic gold in 1972 and 1976 before Cuban lifter Sultan Rakhmanov ended his run at the 1980 Moscow Games. His 600 kg total is now well below what elite super-heavyweights lift, since the press was later dropped from competition and equipment and technique both advanced, but it marked the point where the total lift crossed into new territory.

Muhammad Ali had not lost a professional fight before stepping into Madison Square Garden against Joe Frazier in March 1971, and neither had Frazier, which made this the first meeting between two undefeated heavyweight champions for the title. Ali had spent over three years out of the ring after refusing induction into the army, and the fight doubled as his comeback.

Frazier put Ali down with a left hook in the fifteenth and final round and won a unanimous decision, ending Ali's unbeaten record. Ticket prices, closed-circuit broadcast reach and the two men's combined purses, reportedly 2.5 million dollars each, made it the richest fight staged to that point, and the pair would fight twice more, with Ali winning both.

Skiing at the Olympics had until 1936 meant only cross-country and jumping, the Nordic disciplines favoured by Scandinavian officials who dominated the sport's governing body and were slow to recognise the faster, steeper Alpine style practised in the mountains further south.

Garmisch-Partenkirchen finally staged an Alpine event, a single combined competition scoring downhill and slalom together, open to both men and women. A dispute over the amateur status of ski instructors kept the sport controversial, and separate downhill and slalom medals did not appear until the 1948 Games.

Ban Johnson did not build a new league from nothing in 1901. He had run the minor Western League for years and simply renamed it the American League in 1900, then on 28 January 1901 declared it a major league outright, ignoring the National League's salary cap and raiding its rosters for star players.

The National League fought back before eventually accepting a National Agreement recognising the upstart as an equal, ending a bitter two year trade war between the leagues. The two majors met on the field for the first time in 1903, when the American League's Boston Americans beat the Pittsburgh Pirates in the first modern World Series.

Eleven horses had won the Kentucky Derby and Preakness since Affirmed's 1978 sweep and then failed the Belmont's mile and a half, a distance that punishes horses trained for shorter sprints. American Pharoah, trained by Bob Baffert and ridden by Victor Espinoza, had already won both earlier legs before facing that same test at Belmont Park.

He won by five and a half lengths on 6 June 2015, ending American racing's 37-year wait for a Triple Crown winner and drawing a crowd of over 90,000 to Belmont Park. Baffert had come agonisingly close three times before with other horses, and the win was treated as much a vindication for him as for the colt.

No single decree from 393 CE actually names the Olympic Games. Theodosius I's edicts of the early 390s banned pagan sacrifice and closed temples across the empire, and Olympia's festival, tied to sacrifices at the temple of Zeus, fell under that ban along with countless other local cults. The last Olympiad on record was held that same year, which is why the closure is conventionally dated to 393.

Archaeology complicates the tidy ending: some buildings at Olympia show continued use into the following decades, and a fire that damaged the site around 426 is sometimes credited, without much direct evidence, to a later emperor's order. What is certain is that after roughly 1,170 years the Games stopped, and no continuous successor existed until organisers revived them in Athens in 1896.

The US Anti-Doping Agency issued a report in October 2012 built largely on testimony from Armstrong's own former teammates, including George Hincapie and Floyd Landis, describing a team-wide doping programme run around blood transfusions and EPO through his seven Tour de France wins from 1999 to 2005.

The International Cycling Union accepted the findings and stripped all seven titles, leaving that stretch of the Tour with no official winner rather than promoting runners-up who had also faced doping allegations. Armstrong was banned from competitive cycling for life, and admitted to doping in a televised interview with Oprah Winfrey in January 2013.

Tom Wills and three other members of the newly formed Melbourne Football Club met at the Parade Hotel in 1859 to settle what the loose match a year earlier had lacked: an agreed set of rules that other clubs could play by. They wrote ten in total, borrowing pieces from English rugby and Gaelic football while banning tripping and hacking outright.

Those ten laws allowed catching the ball and running with it, but only if the player bounced or dropped it every so often, an idea that became the bounce still seen in the modern game. The rules spread from Melbourne club to club through the 1860s, giving Australia a football code with no direct equivalent in Britain.

No challenger had beaten the New York Yacht Club in the America's Cup since the trophy was first won in 1851, a run of 132 years across 24 defences. Australia II broke it in Newport, Rhode Island in September 1983, winning the deciding seventh race after trailing three races to one.

The Australian boat carried a winged keel developed in secrecy and disguised under a canvas skirt whenever it was out of the water, prompting protests from the American camp that were ultimately dismissed. Skipper John Bertrand's crew took the Cup back to Perth, ending the longest winning streak in sport at the time.

Axel Paulsen was a speed skater rather than a figure specialist when he entered an 1882 competition in Vienna, and the jump he unveiled there took off forward, off one edge, which no skater had attempted before in competition. Every other jump in the sport takes off backward.

That forward takeoff means the axel requires an extra half rotation compared with jumps of equal name, making it the hardest of figure skating's six jumps to land cleanly. It remains the last jump most skaters master, and the only one still named for the man who first landed it.

Hernan Cortes returned to Spain in 1528 carrying more than gold and reports of conquest. He brought a small group of Mesoamerican performers, among them ballplayers who demonstrated the rubber-ball game ullamaliztli before the court of Charles V. European audiences had never seen a ball that bounced like that, since Europe had no natural rubber of its own.

Players struck the solid rubber ball with hips, thighs or forearms, never hands or feet, competing to keep it moving without letting it touch the ground inside a walled court. Contemporary chroniclers were as struck by the ball's bounce as by the athleticism, and accounts of the demonstration circulated through European courts for years afterward.

Badminton had been an organised English pastime since the 1870s, named for the country house where it was reputedly first played, but had no single body setting rules across countries until nine nations met in 1934 to found the International Badminton Federation.

England, Canada, Denmark, France, Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Scotland and Wales were the founders; the United States joined the following year. The federation renamed itself the Badminton World Federation in 2006 and now governs a sport that reached the Olympics at Barcelona in 1992.

Badminton had appeared once before, as a demonstration sport at the 1972 Munich Games, but Barcelona in 1992 was its first time awarding official medals, with singles and doubles draws for both men and women. Indonesia, which had dominated the sport internationally for years without an Olympic stage to prove it, arrived as the clear favourite.

Susi Susanti beat South Korea's Bang Soo-hyun to win the women's singles final, and about two hours later her fiance Alan Budikusuma won the men's singles title, giving Indonesia its first-ever Olympic gold medals in the same afternoon. The couple married in 1997 and were greeted in Jakarta by a parade reportedly drawing close to a million people.

Giovanni de' Bardi was a count, musician and scholar in Florence when he wrote down the rules of calcio fiorentino in 1580, setting the violent, long-running street game into 33 formal articles for the first time. The game had been played in Florence's piazzas for generations before Bardi bothered to fix it in writing, and his text is the earliest surviving attempt to do so.

Calcio pitted teams of 27 players against each other on a sand-covered piazza, combining elements of football, rugby and wrestling with almost no restriction on where a punch could land. Bardi's rules did little to soften the game, and calcio storico is still played in Florence today in the same brutal spirit his articles described.

Cooperstown, New York was chosen for the Baseball Hall of Fame on the strength of a myth: a 1907 commission credited Abner Doubleday with inventing the game there in 1839, a claim historians have since dismissed, but the centennial date it created stuck and the museum opened on schedule in June 1939.

Five men, Babe Ruth, Honus Wagner, Christy Mathewson, Walter Johnson and Ty Cobb, had already been voted into the first induction class in 1936, three years before the building existed to house their plaques. The hall now holds more than 340 members and remains in the small town the Doubleday story put on the map.

Basketball's Olympic debut at Berlin in 1936 was played outdoors on dirt courts, which turned to mud once rain fell during the final between the United States and Canada; the score finished a low 19-8 to the Americans, a scoreline the sport's inventor James Naismith, present to award the medals, had never seen at that level.

Twenty-three nations entered, evidence the game had already spread well beyond the United States where Naismith had devised it in 1891 with a peach basket and a soccer ball. It has been an Olympic medal sport at every Games since, indoors, ever since.

Bob Beamon's jump in Mexico City was so far past the existing world record, 8.35 metres, that the optical measuring device installed for the competition could not read it; officials had to fetch a tape measure. When his distance, 8.90 metres, was finally announced, Beamon reportedly buckled at the knees and had to be helped up by a teammate.

The leap gained nearly 55 centimetres on the old record in a single jump, an increase track statisticians had assumed would take decades to accumulate. No one beat it for 23 years, until Mike Powell jumped 8.95 metres at the 1991 World Championships in Tokyo in a duel with Carl Lewis.

Simone Biles arrived in Rio de Janeiro in 2016 already unbeaten at world level for three years, and she left with a medal count that matched the hype: gold in the team final, the all-around, vault and floor, plus bronze on balance beam. Only the beam kept her from a clean sweep of every event she entered.

Her all-around margin over the silver medallist, team-mate Aly Raisman, was over two points, an unusually wide gap in a sport normally decided by tenths. Biles was 19, competing in her first Olympics, and her floor routine's difficulty score alone was higher than some rivals managed across their whole set.

Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised gloved fists during the American anthem after finishing first and third in the 200 metres at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, both standing shoeless in black socks. Less noticed at the time was the silver medallist beside them, Australian sprinter Peter Norman, who wore an Olympic Project for Human Rights badge on his own jacket in support.

The International Olympic Committee expelled Smith and Carlos from the Games within two days, and both faced years of hostility at home despite the gesture's later recognition as a defining Olympic image. Norman paid a cost too: Australian officials passed him over for the 1972 Games despite qualifying times good enough to compete, and Smith and Carlos were pallbearers at his 2006 funeral.

Hungary's water polo team learned of the Soviet invasion crushing their country's uprising while already training abroad for the Melbourne Olympics. Weeks later they met the USSR itself in the semi-final, and the match turned physical almost from the start, players trading blows below the waterline out of the referees' view.

The nickname came from Ervin Zador, leaving the pool bleeding from a gash above his eye after a Soviet player struck him late in the game, with Hungary already 4-0 up. Spectators surged toward the pool in fury and police cleared the crowd before the final whistle. Hungary won the match and went on to take the gold medal.

Bobby Jones held a day job as a lawyer and played golf as an amateur, never for prize money, while the best professionals of his era could not beat him. In 1930 he won the US Amateur, the British Amateur, the US Open and the British Open, all four majors then contested, in a single calendar year.

No golfer has repeated the feat, because the majors themselves changed: the Masters and the PGA Championship later replaced the amateur titles in the sport's own definition of a Grand Slam. Jones retired from competition that same year, aged 28, and helped design Augusta National soon after.

England's captain Douglas Jardine had one problem to solve: Don Bradman, who had averaged over 100 in the previous Ashes. His answer was fast bowling aimed at the batsman's body rather than the stumps, with fielders packed on the leg side to catch the defensive deflections it forced.

Australian captain Bill Woodfull was struck above the heart during the third Test, and the Australian board cabled the MCC accusing England of tactics unworthy of the game. The exchange of cables reached both governments before England, having won the series 4-1, agreed to drop the tactic; cricket's laws were rewritten against it soon after.

Fitzstephen's description of winter in London has some boys tying the shin bones of animals under their feet and pushing themselves across the ice of Moorfields with iron-tipped poles, gathering speed until they could cover the length of a field with two strides of momentum. Others staged jousts on the ice and came off worse for it, with broken arms among them.

The bones were not shaped or sharpened like later steel blades. They were flat leg bones, polished smooth by wear, that let a rider glide rather than dig in and push off, which is why poles did most of the propulsion. Archaeologists have since pulled up bone skates matching this description from the Thames and the Fleet.

Jean-Marc Bosman was an unremarkable Belgian midfielder whose contract with RFC Liege expired in 1990, yet the club still demanded a transfer fee to release him to a French second division side, effectively blocking the move and leaving him without a club. Bosman sued, arguing the practice violated European law on freedom of movement for workers.

The European Court of Justice ruled in his favour in December 1995, holding that clubs could not demand a fee for a player whose contract had ended, and that quotas limiting foreign EU players inside domestic leagues were also unlawful. The ruling reshaped football's transfer market almost immediately, driving wages up and shifting bargaining power toward players and their agents, while Bosman's own career never recovered.

There were no gloves and no rounds. Fighters wrapped their hands and forearms in strips of ox-hide leather called himantes, which protected the puncher's knuckles far more than the opponent's face, and a bout at Olympia in 688 BCE ended only when one man could not continue or raised a finger to concede. The first recorded champion was Onomastus of Smyrna, who is credited with writing the event's rules himself.

Blows were allowed to the head only, and there was no ring: fights could range across the open ground until someone yielded. Later Greek boxing added spiked thongs that drew blood far more readily than the softer wraps of 688 BCE. The event stayed on the Olympic programme for centuries and, after Rome absorbed Greek games, its brutal reputation fed directly into gladiatorial spectacle.

Don Bradman walked out at the Oval on 14 August 1948 needing only four runs to finish his Test career with an average of exactly 100. The English crowd gave him three cheers before he faced a ball, and English captain Norman Yardley called for the same. Bradman, visibly moved, was bowled by Eric Hollies for nought two balls later, a googly he apparently never saw.

The duck dropped his average from a projected 101.39 to 99.94, a number now more famous than most centuries in the sport's history. No other batsman with a substantial Test career has come close to it since; the gap between Bradman's average and the next best on record is wider than the gap between second and twentieth.

The change came from the top down rather than by invention: swimmers had been using a butterfly-style overwater arm recovery within breaststroke races for years, and by the 1952 Helsinki Olympics every finalist in the breaststroke events was doing it. FINA's congress, after that Games, narrowly voted to split the single stroke into two, breaststroke and butterfly, each with its own rules.

Butterfly kept the whip kick briefly before separate leg-kick rules followed in 1953, and the stroke did not reach the Olympic programme itself until 1956 in Melbourne. What began as breaststroke swimmers bending the rules to go faster ended up creating one of swimming's four recognised strokes rather than closing the loophole that produced it.

Florence was under siege by the combined forces of Emperor Charles V and Pope Clement VII when its young men staged a calcio match in the Piazza Santa Croce in February 1530, in plain view of the besieging army. It was a deliberate act of defiance, meant to show the enemy that the city was not afraid and had not run short of food or nerve.

Imperial gunners reportedly fired on the piazza during the game rather than stop it, and the match went ahead regardless. Florence fell to the siege later that year, but the game became a fixed part of local memory, and Florentines still play calcio storico in the same piazza each June in period costume.

Malcolm Campbell had already broken the land speed record several times over on English and Welsh beaches, but sand was running out of room for the speeds he wanted. In 1935 he moved his Rolls-Royce-engined Blue Bird to the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, a wider and harder surface.

On 3 September 1935 Campbell was timed at a two-way average of 301.1292 mph, the first car officially recorded above 300 mph. It was his last land speed record; he turned to water speed records afterwards, while his son Donald later broke land and water records of his own.

Bill Russell was still the Celtics' centre in 1966, not yet their coach, when Boston beat the Los Angeles Lakers in seven games for an eighth consecutive title. Red Auerbach had announced before the season that he would retire from coaching once it ended, and Russell took the job for the following year, becoming the first Black head coach of a major North American professional sports team.

No other team in the four major North American leagues has matched an eight-year championship run. Boston's streak had begun in 1959 and would end the next season, when the 76ers beat them in the conference finals, but the Celtics regrouped and won two more titles in 1968 and 1969 with Russell now coaching as well as playing.

Chester's races began on the Roodee, a flat meadow beside the city walls named for a stone cross once standing on what had been an island in the Dee. The city's mayor, Henry Gee, is credited with organising the first recorded race there on 10 January 1539, offering a silver bell to whichever horse's owner won it, after the traditional Shrovetide football match had grown too violent to tolerate.

Guinness World Records credits Chester with the longest continuous history of any racecourse on earth. Racing has not run every single year, wars and outbreaks interrupted the calendar more than once, but the Roodee has kept hosting meetings on the same ground for close to five centuries, longer than any other track can claim.

Every other baseball club in 1869 still pretended to be amateur, paying players quietly under the table while claiming otherwise. Harry Wright, the Red Stockings' English-born manager, dropped the pretence and put ten men on salary openly, the first club to do so.

The team then travelled roughly 12,000 miles by rail that season, playing exhibition games from Massachusetts to California and finishing unbeaten. The run ended the following year, but the tour had already shown promoters that a fully professional club could draw paying crowds nationwide.

Rome's oldest entertainment venue began as a marked-out track in a marshy valley between the Palatine and Aventine hills, laid out under the Etruscan king Tarquinius Priscus around 600 BCE. Tradition credits him with staging chariot races there to mark the capture of a neighbouring town, using only temporary wooden seating.

It took centuries of rebuilding before the Circus Maximus reached the stone form associated with imperial Rome, eventually holding a claimed 150,000 spectators. Even at its earliest and crudest, the valley's shape, long and narrow with a turning post at each end, fixed the template every Roman circus later copied. Chariot racing there outlasted the Republic, the Empire, and Rome's pagan religion.

The claim rests on a single charter: a 1297 document from Loenen aan de Vecht, near Utrecht, that records a game called colf played to mark the anniversary of the town gate's destruction four years earlier. It is the oldest documentary trace of the game anywhere in the Low Countries, which is why golf histories keep returning to it.

Colf was played with a leather ball and a wooden club toward a chosen target such as a door or a tree, over open ground rather than a laid-out course, closer to a cross-country target game than to a links round. It fed into two later Dutch pastimes, kolf on ice and kolf indoors, both distinct from the game the Scots eventually standardised.

The Colosseum's opening in 80 CE was not a single afternoon but a hundred-day festival, staged by the emperor Titus to mark the amphitheatre's completion and, unofficially, to secure his own popularity after inheriting the throne from his father Vespasian. Gladiatorial duels ran alongside staged hunts using animals shipped in from across the empire.

Roman writers claim thousands of animals were killed across the hundred days, and some accounts describe the arena floor being flooded for mock naval battles, though how that flooding actually worked with the Colosseum's later underground chambers remains debated among archaeologists. Titus reportedly wept during the closing ceremony, according to the historian Suetonius, apparently moved by the scale of what he had just given Rome.

This was not a spontaneous brawl but an arranged fight, agreed in advance between the French garrison at Josselin and the English-allied garrison at Ploermel during the Breton War of Succession. Thirty knights and squires a side met on open ground between the two castles and fought on foot with swords, axes and daggers until one side yielded.

The Franco-Breton side won, and several of its captains, including Jean de Beaumanoir, became celebrated figures in chivalric writing for centuries afterward. It was treated at the time less as a battle than as a formal trial of honour, and it is still commemorated with a monument standing on the site in Brittany.

When Constantine dedicated his new capital in 330 CE, the Hippodrome he completed there was not new construction from nothing; an earlier arena had stood on the site since the reign of Septimius Severus over a century before. Constantine enlarged and finished it, adding an imperial viewing box connected directly to the palace so the emperor could watch chariot races without entering the public stands.

For the next thousand years the Hippodrome was far more than a racetrack. Byzantine emperors used the crowd's factional loyalties, the Blues and the Greens, as a barometer of political support, and in 532 a dispute among race fans escalated into the Nika riots, which killed tens of thousands and nearly toppled Justinian's reign.

Fausto Coppi had already dominated the Giro d'Italia through the 1940s, but the Tour de France was a race he had never finished before 1949. That July he won it outright, having taken the Giro two months earlier, becoming the first rider to hold both titles in the same season. His rival and teammate Gino Bartali, twelve years the older man, still finished second in both races that year.

The double was not repeated by anyone else for another decade, and only a handful of riders have managed it since, most recently Marco Pantani in 1998. Coppi's 1949 season is usually treated as the moment road cycling's centre of gravity shifted decisively from prewar Italy's Bartali toward a faster, more aggressive style Coppi rode for most of the following decade.

Cricket between counties had been played for over a century before anyone made it a formal competition. In December 1889 county secretaries meeting in London agreed a points system, and in 1890 the English County Championship was constituted with eight counties competing for a title decided on results rather than reputation.

Surrey won that first season, finishing above Lancashire on the new points table after a summer in which the champions lost only one match. The competition it created still runs every English summer, and its early scoring quirks, including matches that counted for less if rain shortened them, were argued over for decades afterward.

Lynne Cox had wanted to swim the Bering Strait since 1976, but Cold War border restrictions kept Soviet officials from answering her requests for eleven years. She finally crossed on 7 August 1987, from Little Diomede Island in Alaska to Big Diomede on the Soviet side, wearing only a swimsuit in water just above freezing.

The swim took two hours and sixteen minutes and crossed the international date line as well as the maritime border, a gap of about 2.7 miles that had effectively separated two nations for decades. Four months later, Mikhail Gorbachev raised a toast to Cox at the White House signing of the INF Treaty, crediting the swim with easing tension between the two countries.

The Neo Phaliron velodrome had been finished only weeks before the 1896 Athens Games opened, and cycling was one of the new sports slotted into Pierre de Coubertin's revived Olympics from the start. Six events were held there and on the roads around the city, mixing sprint races with a punishing 12 hour endurance ride.

France's Paul Masson won three of the track titles, while the road race to Marathon and back was won by a Greek rider, Aristidis Konstantinidis, in front of a home crowd. Cycling has appeared at every summer Games since, one of the few sports with an unbroken record stretching back to that first Athens programme.

Henri Desgrange is remembered today for founding the Tour de France, but in 1893 he was still a competitive rider chasing a record nobody had yet formalised. On 11 May he rode alone at the Buffalo velodrome near Paris for sixty minutes, covering 35.325 kilometres, the first distance recognised as an official hour record.

The mark stood for barely a year before being broken, unlike the Tour he would later create. What Desgrange fixed permanently was the format itself: a solo rider against the clock on a track, no pacing, no draft, a contest so stripped down that more than a century of successors, including Eddy Merckx and Chris Boardman, are still judged against the same rule.

Diagoras of Rhodes had been an Olympic boxing champion himself decades earlier. In 448 BCE he watched both of his sons win Olympic titles on the same day, one in boxing and one in pankration, and the crowd's response became the scene later writers kept retelling: the two young champions lifted their elderly father onto their shoulders and carried him around the stadium while spectators showered him with flowers.

A Spartan in the crowd is said to have called out that Diagoras should die on the spot, since there was nothing left in life worth living for, and according to the story he did die shortly afterward, contented. The tale may be embellished, but Diagoras's family kept producing champions across three generations, making his line one of the most successful athletic dynasties recorded from the ancient Games.

The jump itself was a triple loop, not just any triple, and Dick Button had spent months building toward it deliberately: he first landed it in practice in Boston in December 1951, then showed it publicly at an exhibition in Vienna before risking it at the Olympics themselves. At Oslo in February 1952 he landed it in competition, a jump no skater had attempted at that level before.

Button was already the reigning Olympic champion from 1948, and Oslo made him the first skater to win back-to-back men's Olympic titles as well as the first to land a triple in competition. He later became one of American television's most recognisable skating commentators, a second career that outlasted his competitive one by decades.

A stone inscription set up in Rome in 146 CE, now catalogued as CIL 6.10048, records the full career of the charioteer Gaius Appuleius Diocles: 24 years of racing, 4,257 starts, 1,462 wins, and lifetime winnings of 35,863,120 sesterces. He retired at 42, having raced for the White, Green and finally Red factions after starting his career in Lusitania, in what is now Portugal and Spain.

That sum has been estimated as enough to feed the entire city of Rome for a year, and roughly five times what a provincial governor might expect to earn over a comparable stretch. The figure comes from admirers who erected the inscription themselves rather than from any official Roman record, but even generously discounted it makes Diocles a strong candidate for history's highest-paid athlete, chariot racing or otherwise.

Professionals had been barred from Olympic basketball for decades, a rule that let the Soviet Union's veteran squad beat an amateur US college team in 1988. FIBA lifted the ban in 1989, and the United States responded by sending active NBA players for the first time, a roster assembled specifically to reclaim the gold it had just lost.

Michael Jordan, Magic Johnson, Larry Bird, Charles Barkley and Patrick Ewing were among twelve players who won every game in Barcelona by an average margin above 43 points, drawing bigger crowds for their practices than for other nations' actual matches. Opposing teams reportedly asked for autographs and photos before tip-off rather than treating the games as contests.

The record is a property dispute, not a sports report. In a 1598 Guildford court case over a patch of common land, a 59-year-old coroner named John Derrick testified that around fifty years earlier, as a schoolboy at the Free School, he and his friends had played 'creckett' there, along with other games, giving the sport its earliest known written mention anywhere.

Derrick's testimony pushes the game's origin back to roughly 1550, decades before any match report exists, and it survives purely because a lawsuit needed to establish how long the land had been used for play. Cricket historians still cite this single deposition as the firmest anchor for when the sport began in England.

Eclipse's owner, Dennis O'Kelly, is credited with summing up every one of his races in five words: Eclipse first, the rest nowhere. The horse ran eighteen races between 1769 and 1770, all under punishing four-mile heat formats, and finished so far ahead each time that few owners bothered entering against him after his first few starts.

His real influence came after retirement, at stud rather than on the track. Roughly nine in ten thoroughbreds racing today trace their male line back to Eclipse, a concentration no other eighteenth-century sire matched, which is why his skeleton is still kept and studied by the Royal Veterinary College.

Gertrude Ederle had already failed one Channel crossing attempt in 1925 before succeeding on 6 August 1926, swimming from Cap Gris-Nez in France to Kingsdown in England despite rough seas that pushed her off course for miles. She used a crawl stroke rather than the breaststroke most earlier Channel swimmers favoured.

Her time, just under 14 hours and 34 minutes, beat the existing men's record by close to two hours, not merely matched it. Ederle returned to New York to a ticker-tape parade with an estimated two million people lining the route, a scale of welcome no female athlete had received before her.

Sumo had been staged for centuries before 1684, mostly as festival entertainment or a fundraising draw for shrines. What changed at Tomioka Hachiman was permission: the shogunate had banned unlicensed public sumo after earlier bouts ended in brawls, so a formal kanjin licence, granted to fifteen named rikishi, meant paid, regulated matches could resume in Edo.

Ikazuchi Gondayu headed the group that received the permit, and the Tomioka Hachiman shrine still marks the event with a monument listing every yokozuna since. The licensing system that began here, tying professional sumo to shrine fundraising and shogunal oversight, shaped how the sport was organised in Japan for the next two centuries.

Edward II's proclamation was not aimed at sport as such but at disorder: it complained that large crowds pushing a ball through the streets caused riots and might mask a breach of the king's peace. Anyone caught playing within the City of London risked imprisonment, and it was issued in the king's name by the mayor.

It was the first of a long English tradition of royal bans on mob football, repeated by Edward III, Richard II and Henry IV over the following century, none of them lasting. Games kept being played in streets and fields regardless, because there was no police force capable of enforcing a ban on a crowd sport.

Edward III's writ ordered every able-bodied man to practise with the longbow on Sundays and holidays, and pointedly forbade football, handball, cock-fighting and other games that were drawing men away from the butts. It was issued during a lull in the Hundred Years' War, when England's military edge depended on a supply of trained archers rather than mounted knights.

The law had teeth because towns kept archery butts as a civic obligation and constables could fine men who skipped practice. English longbowmen went on to win Crecy, Poitiers and later Agincourt, and historians treat statutes like this one as part of why England could field so many skilled archers rather than relying on continental crossbowmen.

The scores were level at 17-17 deep into extra time in Sydney when Matt Dawson passed to Jonny Wilkinson just inside Australia's 22. Wilkinson struck the drop goal with his weaker right foot, the ball clearing the crossbar with twenty seconds left on the clock, and Australia never got possession back.

It remains the only Rugby World Cup won by a northern hemisphere team, and the only one England have won. Wilkinson had missed a similar chance earlier in the match, and coach Clive Woodward had built the win on a squad drilled for years around exactly that kind of pressure kick rather than open, running rugby.

Geoff Hurst's second goal, the one that put England 3-2 up, is still argued over: the ball struck the underside of the crossbar and bounced down, and television replays have never settled whether it crossed the line. The Soviet linesman signalled a goal, the referee agreed, and it stood. No dispute attaches to Hurst's third, a clean strike into the top corner in the final seconds.

Hurst remains the only player to score a hat-trick in a men's World Cup final. Bobby Moore lifted the trophy as captain, and commentator Kenneth Wolstenholme's line as fans spilled onto the Wembley pitch, some people are on the pitch, they think it's all over, it is now, became the most quoted sentence in English football.

Equestrian sport entered the Olympics at Stockholm in 1912 with dressage, eventing and show jumping all on the programme together for the first time. Entry was restricted to commissioned military officers riding their own horses, a rule that shut out civilians and, in most competing nations, women entirely.

The military-officer restriction persisted for decades and was not fully lifted until the 1950s, after which equestrian became one of the few Olympic sports where men and women compete directly against each other in the same events. Sweden, hosting in 1912, won the inaugural team eventing title.

Speed skating at the 1980 Lake Placid Olympics covered five distances, from the sprint of 500 metres to the endurance test of 10,000 metres, disciplines usually split between sprinters and distance specialists. Eric Heiden, a 21-year-old from Wisconsin, entered as a favourite in most of them but was not expected to sweep every one.

He won all five, setting an Olympic record in each and a world record in the 10,000 metres despite having little experience racing that far. No skater, male or female, has won five individual golds at a single Winter Olympics since. Heiden later became an orthopaedic surgeon and worked with US Olympic teams rather than continuing in the sport he had dominated.

James V had the court at Falkland Palace built between 1539 and 1541 as part of his renovation of the palace into a French-style retreat, giving Scotland's monarchy a private venue for a game that was already fashionable at continental courts. It is a jeu quarre design, roofless and rectangular, unlike the more common covered jeu a dedans courts found elsewhere in Europe.

It is the oldest real tennis court still in use anywhere, though not continuously played on since the sixteenth century. Mary, Queen of Scots is recorded as an enthusiastic player there, and the court has since been restored and is maintained by a modern club that still plays on its original stone-flagged surface.

Juan Manuel Fangio was 46 years old when he won his fifth Formula One drivers' championship in 1957, driving a Maserati after a single season away from Mercedes. He had already won titles with three different manufacturers, a feat that alone set him apart from every driver who followed.

His fifth title was the record for 46 years, outlasting most of the sport's postwar history, until Michael Schumacher overtook it in 2003 on his way to a seventh. Fangio retired the following year, in 1958, having started 51 grands prix and won 24 of them, a win rate no other champion has matched.

Delegates from Belgium, France and the Netherlands met in Liege in 1881 to found the European Gymnastics Federation, a body meant to standardise a sport that had grown up separately in gymnastics societies across the continent. It renamed itself the Federation Internationale de Gymnastique in 1921 once its reach became global.

That makes it the oldest international sports federation still operating, older than the International Olympic Committee by more than a decade. It went on to organise gymnastics at the first modern Olympics in 1896 and still sets the code of points judges use today.

Swimming at the 1908 London Olympics was run under rules that varied by country, with no single body to settle disputes over strokes or eligibility between events. Delegates from eight national federations met during the Games and founded the Federation Internationale de Natation to standardise competition worldwide.

FINA took over swimming, diving and water polo, and later added synchronised swimming and open water events as they developed. It kept its French-derived name and Olympic-linked founding for over a century before rebranding as World Aquatics in 2023, a name change rather than any shift in what it governs.

The race was designed less to crown the fastest car over one lap than to test which manufacturer's cars could survive a full day and night of hard use on public roads outside Le Mans. Andre Lagache and Rene Leonard shared a Chenard-Walcker to win the first running in 1923, covering just over 2,200 kilometres.

Early editions were run as part of a three-year Triple Crown, with the winner decided by combined distance across successive years rather than a single race, a rule long since dropped. The 24-hour format itself survived every change to the regulations and remains the race's defining feature more than a century later.

Kwame Nkrumah had pushed for an African Games since the late 1950s, but it took Congolese president Fulbert Youlou's offer of Brazzaville, and years of funding trouble, to get one on the calendar. Fewer than a decade after most of the continent left colonial rule, the event doubled as a statement that African nations could stage major sport themselves.

Athletics, boxing, football, basketball and cycling filled a week of competition, with Ethiopian and Egyptian runners among the standouts on the track. The Games were meant to run every four years; political upheaval, funding gaps and boycotts scattered the schedule instead, and a second edition did not follow until 1973, in Lagos.

There was no singles competition at the first All England Championships. The tournament, held on 4 April 1899 at a drill hall in Westminster, offered only doubles events: men's, women's and mixed. Singles titles were not added to the programme until the following year, once the format had proven itself worth repeating.

D. W. Oakes was the busiest player on the day, winning the men's doubles alongside Stewart Marsden Massey and the mixed doubles with Daisy St John, while Meriel Lucas and Mary Graeme took the women's doubles. The championship became badminton's most prestigious open event and the oldest still contested, run in London every year with only wartime gaps.

The trophy did not yet carry that name in 1851. The schooner America, built by a New York syndicate, sailed to England and beat a fleet of British yachts around the Isle of Wight for a trophy then called the £100 Cup, awarded by the Royal Yacht Squadron.

The syndicate later donated the cup to the New York Yacht Club under a deed of gift specifying it be held as a trophy for international competition, and it was renamed the America's Cup after the winning boat. The first defence under that name did not happen until 1870, but the race that created the trophy is the one from 1851.

The 1903 gathering in Antwerp was not billed as a world championship at the time. It ran alongside a Belgian gymnastics festival, and only later did the sport's governing body retroactively label it the first Artistic Gymnastics World Championships, with four European nations sending men's teams.

There was no individual champion crowned that year; scoring was purely by team, and an all-round individual title did not appear until 1922. Belgium, hosting, competed against France, the Netherlands and a fourth nation, in a format closer to a national display than the multi-apparatus spectacle the championships became.

The first Asian Games were meant to open in 1950 but were pushed back a year, and New Delhi hosted them in March 1951 with 489 athletes from eleven nations, a modest field compared with the thousands the event now draws. The idea had been discussed since the 1940s among Asian sporting officials keen to build a regional counterpart to the Olympics rather than rely on European-run competitions.

India dominated the medal table at its own Games, and the event ran without some nations, including Pakistan, still working out how newly drawn borders affected sporting federations. Eight sports made the first programme, a fraction of the roughly forty now contested, and the Games have run every four years since, war and boycotts aside.

The 1905 championships in Melbourne were a joint Australian and New Zealand event from the start, run by the two nations' lawn tennis associations before either country had its own separate national title. Rodney Heath won the men's singles on the grass courts of the Warehousemen's Cricket Ground.

The tournament rotated between Australian and New Zealand cities for decades, only becoming a purely Australian championship, and eventually the Australian Open, once the two associations split their competitions in the 1920s. Melbourne has hosted it far more often than any other city.

Scotch College and Melbourne Grammar met on a paddock near the Yarra River in 1858 with no fixed rulebook at all: each side simply agreed on the day how many players would take part and how long they would play, and the match ran across three Saturdays without a clear winner.

It is remembered less for its result than for who watched it. Tom Wills, a cricketer who had grown up around Aboriginal ball games and wanted footballers fit for summer, helped organise the game, and the following year he was one of the men who wrote down the first formal rules for what became Australian rules football.

The Knickerbockers had drawn up their own rulebook that spring, fixing a diamond-shaped infield, foul lines and the idea of tagging runners out instead of throwing the ball at them, a practice called soaking that had bruised too many players. When they finally played a match under those rules at the Elysian Fields on 19 June 1846, they lost.

The New York Nine beat them 23 to 1 in four innings, a scoreline the Knickerbockers' own club secretary, Alexander Cartwright, recorded as umpire that day. Later research has complicated the game's claim to being truly the first of its kind, but it remains the earliest baseball match for which a box score under written rules survives.

The machines racing through the Parc de Saint-Cloud on 31 May 1868 were wooden-framed velocipedes with iron-rimmed wheels and no gears or pneumatic tyres, nicknamed boneshakers for what riding one over cobbles felt like. The course was a short, flat sprint of roughly 1,200 metres, closer to a park stroll than a modern race distance.

James Moore, an English student living in Paris, won it, and two years later he also won the first Paris to Rouen road race, a far longer test that helped set cycling on course to become a competitive sport with organised long-distance events rather than a park novelty.

Judging a man on physique alone, with no lifting or strength test attached, was itself the novelty. Eugen Sandow, already famous as a Victorian strongman and showman, filled the Royal Albert Hall on 14 September 1901 for a contest built purely to reward how competitors looked rather than what they could lift.

Sandow judged alongside the sculptor Charles Lawes and the author Arthur Conan Doyle, breaking ties himself when the other two disagreed. William Murray of Nottingham won the top prize of over a thousand pounds. The contest is generally treated as bodybuilding's first true show, separating physique display from strength sport for good.

Hamilton, Ontario put up the money to host the first British Empire Games in 1930 after other cities balked at the cost, and the city built a stadium for the occasion. Eleven countries sent about 400 athletes, competing in six sports, a fraction of the scale the Games would later reach.

The event was renamed the British Empire and Commonwealth Games in 1954, then simply the Commonwealth Games in 1978, as the language of empire fell away from the title while the competition itself kept running every four years. England won the most medals at that first meeting.

No union back home organised this trip. Two entrepreneurs, Arthur Shaw and Alfred Shrewsbury, put the squad together as a money-making venture, and it sailed from England in March 1888 without any blessing from the Rugby Football Union. Captain Robert Seddon drowned in a rowing accident on the tour and never saw it finish.

The team played thirty-five matches across five months in New Zealand and Australia, winning twenty-seven, and also picked up a sideline in Victorian rules football to fill the calendar. No Test matches were played, since no touring side yet carried that status, but the itinerary became the template every Lions tour since has followed.

The teams that met at Rutgers on 6 November 1869 were not playing anything a modern fan would recognise. Twenty-five men a side kicked a round ball toward the opponent's goal; catching or carrying it was against the rules, unlike the code Walter Camp would later rewrite into American football.

Rutgers won 6-4 on home turf, and Princeton demanded a rematch under its own rules a week later, which Princeton won. The two schools then dropped the sport for several years after faculty at both objected to the disorder it caused among students.

The BCS had picked a national title matchup by computer formula and human polls for sixteen years, and coaches, fans and sportswriters spent nearly as long arguing that a two-team pairing could not settle a fair champion among dozens of unbeaten claims. A four-team playoff, seeded by a selection committee rather than a formula, replaced it starting in the 2014 season.

Ohio State entered as a committee-selected fourth seed behind Alabama, Oregon and Florida State, then beat Alabama in the semifinal and Oregon in the title game in January 2015. The result was treated as vindication for the committee's judgement over a formula, and the four-team format ran for a decade before expanding further in 2024.

Vic Clapham, a First World War veteran, proposed the race between Pietermaritzburg and Durban to honour soldiers who had marched similar distances on campaign. Only 34 men started on Empire Day, 1921, running roughly 89 kilometres over the Natal hills, and 16 of them finished.

Bill Rowan won in eight hours and 59 minutes, more than 40 minutes ahead of the runner-up, Harry Phillips. His name is now attached to the medal every finisher under nine hours still receives, and the race he won alone in 1921 draws around 20,000 entrants each year.

The tournament that became the Copa America was staged in Buenos Aires to mark a century since Argentina's independence, not as a planned annual fixture. Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil and Chile entered, and Uruguay won every match to take the first title, a result that set the pattern for the competition's early decades.

It ran a full eight years before the first FIFA World Cup and predates the European championship by more than four decades, which makes it the oldest continental football tournament still played. It has changed format and name more than once since 1916, but the four founding nations still anchor the field.

One-day cricket was barely a decade old as a serious format when England hosted the first men's World Cup in June 1975, sponsored by an insurance company and known as the Prudential Cup. Eight teams played 60-over matches, a length now considered marathon by modern one-day standards.

West Indies reached the final at Lord's against Australia, and captain Clive Lloyd scored 102 off 85 balls, an innings built on power rather than caution. West Indies won by 17 runs after the match ran close to nine hours. The tournament proved one-day cricket could draw crowds and money on its own, separate from Test matches.

Dwight Davis was a Harvard student, not yet the celebrated diplomat he later became, when he paid for a silver trophy out of his own pocket and persuaded the British to send a team to Boston in August 1900. He also played in the tie he had organised, winning the opening singles rubber himself at the Longwood Cricket Club.

The United States won 3-0, with Malcolm Whitman beating a young Arthur Gore, who would later win Wimbledon three times, before Davis and Holcombe Ward sealed the tie in doubles. The contest was called the International Lawn Tennis Challenge at first; it only picked up Davis's own name informally, long before it became the sport's official team competition.

The new Daytona International Speedway opened with a race so close that officials could not tell who had won it. Lee Petty and Johnny Beauchamp crossed the line together at the end of 500 miles, and Beauchamp was initially declared the winner on the track.

It took three days of study, including newsreel footage submitted by a spectator, before NASCAR reversed the call and awarded the race to Petty. The photo finish became part of the speedway's founding legend. Petty's son Richard later won the same race a record seven times.

Eugene Rubens-Alcais, a deaf French athlete and journalist, organised the first International Silent Games in Paris in 1924, drawing around 145 competitors from nine countries. It ran under its own federation rather than any Olympic body, since deaf athletes had no route into the mainstream games at the time.

Events covered athletics, swimming, cycling and football, judged and officiated largely by deaf organisers themselves. The Games have run roughly every four years since, renamed the Deaflympics in 2001, making 1924 the start of the second-oldest continuous multi-sport event after the modern Olympics.

The competition almost did not survive its own launch. English football's authorities were hostile to the idea and the Football League barred champions Chelsea from entering, wary of fixture congestion and continental travel, so it fell to French sports paper L'Equipe's push for the tournament to prove its worth without England.

Real Madrid's 4-3 win over Stade de Reims at the Parc des Princes settled that question. Reims led twice before Madrid's Alfredo Di Stefano and Hector Rial turned the final, and Madrid went on to win the first five European Cups, establishing the club and the competition together.

Spain was drawn against the Soviet Union in the quarter-finals of the first European Nations' Cup but General Franco's government refused to let the team travel, unwilling to face a communist state, so the Soviets advanced without playing a match. West Germany and Italy both skipped the tournament entirely, unconvinced it mattered.

Only four teams reached the finals in France. The Soviet Union beat Yugoslavia 2-1 after extra time in the final in Paris, with Viktor Ponedelnik scoring the winner. The competition was renamed the European Championship in 1968 and grew into the continental tournament played every four years today.

ESPN had spent two years developing a television event around sports it judged underrepresented on mainstream broadcast, skateboarding, BMX, inline skating, sport climbing and bungee jumping among them, before staging the first Extreme Games across nine days in Newport and Providence, Rhode Island, in June 1995.

Roughly 200,000 spectators attended in person, a figure that surprised even ESPN's own planners, and the broadcast reached an audience large enough to justify a second edition the following year. The event was renamed the X Games in 1996 and later added a separate winter version, becoming a fixture of ESPN's programming rather than the one-off experiment it started as.

The race that opened the Formula One World Championship was held on a former airfield, Silverstone still ringed with wartime concrete and hangars in 1950. Nino Farina won it for Alfa Romeo on 13 May, leading an Alfa clean sweep of the podium ahead of teammates Luigi Fagioli and Juan Manuel Fangio, whose own championship years were still to come.

King George VI attended, along with a crowd estimated well into the six figures, drawn as much by prewar motor-racing nostalgia as by the novelty of a new championship. Alfa Romeo's 158, a supercharged straight-eight dating back to before the war, won every round of that first season; nobody realised yet that the championship's first year would also be the last for a car that old.

Basketball's first world championship was played entirely in one city, Buenos Aires, with ten national teams and no qualifying rounds beyond simply agreeing to travel. Argentina, playing at home in front of large and vocal crowds, beat the United States in the deciding match to take the title, a result the heavily favoured Americans had not expected.

The United States had sent college players rather than its strongest available amateurs, and FIBA's early tournaments carried nothing like the prestige the Olympic basketball tournament already had. Argentina's win was nonetheless the first world title the sport had ever crowned outside the Olympics, three years before the tournament found a fixed four-year cycle.

Scotland picked its side entirely from one club, Queen's Park, because no national association yet existed to select more widely. England's team was drawn largely from southern amateur clubs, and around 4,000 spectators paid a shilling each to watch at Hamilton Crescent, the West of Scotland cricket ground.

Neither side managed a goal, but the match mattered for what it proved rather than what it produced: that a fixture between nations could be organised, refereed and repeated. The fixture became annual and is now recognised by FIFA as the first official international football match.

The tournament that became the French Open opened as something much narrower: a men's singles event restricted to members of French tennis clubs, played in Paris in 1891. Foreign players were shut out entirely, which meant none of the era's leading British or American names could enter even if they had wanted to.

H. Briggs won that first men's title. The championship stayed a closed, national affair for decades, only opening to international entrants in 1925, and it did not move to the clay courts of Stade Roland Garros until 1928, when it needed a stadium big enough for a Davis Cup crowd.

The race that gave the world the term grand prix was run over two brutal days near Le Mans in June 1906, six laps of a 103 kilometre circuit each day, well over a marathon of racing in total. The tar-and-gravel surface melted in the heat and burned drivers' eyes as it flicked up from the wheels ahead.

Ferenc Szisz, a Hungarian mechanic-turned-driver for Renault, won by roughly half an hour over Felice Nazzaro. Renault's car had detachable rims that let its pit crew change a tyre in minutes rather than the quarter of an hour rivals needed, a decisive edge over a race lasting nearly 1,240 kilometres.

La Gazzetta dello Sport launched the Giro in 1909 largely to outsell its rival paper Corriere della Sera, which had already backed the Giro di Lombardia. The first edition ran eight stages and roughly 2,400 kilometres from Milan, with points awarded by finishing position rather than time, so a rider could win overall without winning a single stage.

Luigi Ganna, a bricklayer turned cyclist, took the overall title despite winning only two of the eight stages outright. He reportedly told journalists asking how he felt that his backside was destroyed, a line that has stuck to the race's founding story ever since.

John L. Sullivan had built his fame on bare-knuckle prize fighting, so his last title defence, in New Orleans on 7 September 1892, was fought under the Marquess of Queensberry rules, with gloves and three-minute rounds rather than bare fists and no time limit. James J. Corbett, younger and far quicker, was the challenger.

Corbett knocked Sullivan out in the twenty-first round to take the title, ending a run that had made Sullivan the first genuine national sports celebrity in the United States. The fight is usually cited as the moment the gloved, timed version of boxing that survives today replaced the bare-knuckle era at the top of the sport.

Whether 1839 was really the first running is argued over even now: similar steeplechases had been held at Aintree and nearby Maghull from 1836, but those earlier races drew little attention and were largely forgotten, letting the 1839 race stand as the event's official start. Seventeen horses lined up at Aintree on 26 February that year.

Lottery, ridden by Jem Mason, won what was then called the Liverpool Grand Steeplechase over a course already featuring the ditches and banks that evolved into fences still jumped today, including what became known as Becher's Brook after a rider who fell into it in an earlier race. The result gave the fixture, later renamed the Grand National, its first official winner.

Athens already held an annual festival for its patron goddess Athena, but in 566 BCE the statesman Pisistratus expanded it into a grander event held every fourth year, the Great Panathenaia, with athletic contests modelled to rival Olympia's prestige. Winners did not receive olive wreaths as at Olympia; they were given large ceramic amphorae filled with sacred oil pressed from Athena's own olive trees.

The oil itself had real value, since a single amphora could be sold or used for years, unlike a wreath that withered within days. Surviving Panathenaic amphorae, painted with the goddess on one side and the relevant event on the other, are now one of the best sources historians have for what Greek sport actually looked like.

The Grey Cup exists because a departing governor general wanted to leave a mark on Canadian sport. Earl Grey donated the trophy in 1909 for the Dominion's amateur football championship, and the University of Toronto won the first final, beating the Toronto Parkdale Canoe Club 26-6 at Rosedale Field.

For its early decades the cup belonged to amateur and university teams rather than professionals, and it took until the 1950s to become the championship of a fully professional Canadian Football League. It remains one of the oldest continuously awarded trophies in North American team sport.

The trophy Jay Berwanger won in 1935 was not yet the Heisman. New York's Downtown Athletic Club had just created an award for the best college football player east of the Mississippi, then opened it nationwide, and Berwanger, a halfback for the University of Chicago, was its first winner.

Berwanger never played in the NFL: the Chicago Bears drafted him first overall in the league's inaugural draft, but he turned professional football down over pay and became a coach and businessman instead. The award was renamed for the club's late athletic director, John Heisman, the year after Berwanger won it.

The 1839 regatta grew out of a town meeting in Henley aimed at raising money and drawing visitors, not out of any rowing club's ambition. Local worthies organised a programme of races on the reach of the Thames already made familiar by the Oxford and Cambridge boat race a decade earlier, and it drew a large enough crowd to be repeated the next year.

Prince Albert lent his patronage in 1851, turning it into the Royal Regatta and giving it the prestige that attracted international crews. Held every summer since, with breaks only for the two world wars, Henley grew from a one-off fundraiser into one of rowing's most prestigious annual fixtures.

England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales had already been playing occasional rugby internationals for over a decade before anyone organised the results into a proper table. The 1883 season was the first counted as a championship, decided on match results between the four unions rather than as a single tournament.

England won that first championship outright, and the competition kept expanding as it aged: France joined in 1910, Italy in 2000, turning it into today's Six Nations. It is the oldest international rugby competition still contested, its early results still recognised as the championship's origin.

The match organised by James Creighton at Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink on 3 March 1875 used nine players a side and a flat wooden disc rather than the ball or lacrosse puck field games used outdoors, chosen specifically so it would not fly into spectators or shatter windows.

The Montreal Gazette reported the next day that around 40 people watched, and that the game ended in a brawl once players and onlookers began disputing the rough play. Despite the disorder, the fixed rules, timed periods and goaltenders on show make it the earliest recorded organised ice hockey game.

No franchise entering the first Indian Premier League auction in 2008 had a track record to bid against, since the league itself did not exist yet. Owners paid for players on reputation and Twenty20 form alone, and Rajasthan Royals, the cheapest franchise sold, built a squad around Shane Warne as captain rather than star batting names.

Warne's Royals lost their opening match, then won eleven of the next twelve to reach the final in Navi Mumbai, where they beat Chennai Super Kings by three wickets in a chase completed with an over to spare. The result gave the fledgling league an underdog story in its very first season, which did more for its popularity than any of the bigger-name franchises could have.

The idea came out of an argument among Hawaii athletes over which was harder: swimming, cycling or running. A naval officer named John Collins proposed settling it by combining the island's three existing endurance races, a 2.4-mile swim, a 112-mile bike ride and a full marathon, into one day, on 18 February 1978.

Fifteen men started on Oahu; twelve finished. Gordon Haller, a taxi driver and former navy man, won in 11 hours 46 minutes 58 seconds, edging Dave Orlowski over the final miles of the run. The race relocated to Kailua-Kona the next year and grew into the Ironman World Championship, now contested by thousands each October.

The first Tourist Trophy in 1907 was created because Britain's mainland roads were legally closed to racing under a 20 mph limit. The Isle of Man's own parliament could suspend that limit, so organisers moved the race there, over a shortened 15-mile St John's course rather than the full mountain circuit used later.

Charlie Collier won the single-cylinder class on a Matchless, averaging under 40 mph, and a twin-cylinder class ran separately with a fuel-consumption rule meant to encourage practical road machines. The race grew into the mountain-course TT still run today, but that first edition was closer to a fuel-economy trial than a modern race.

Kabaddi has no ball, no bat and no equipment at all beyond a marked court. A raider crosses into the opposing half chanting a single breath's worth of syllables, tries to touch defenders and get back before the breath runs out, and the entire contest of strength happens in that one held lungful of air.

The International Kabaddi Federation staged the first World Cup in Mumbai in November 2004, using the Standard style rather than the Circle style played across South Asian villages. India beat Iran 55-27 in the final, a lopsided score typical of a sport where India had produced most of the world's elite players for decades.

Thirty-three riders started the first Liège-Bastogne-Liège on 29 May 1892, sent out on a 250 kilometre loop from Liège down to Bastogne and back over roads that were barely more than farm tracks. It was organised by a local cycling club rather than any national federation, an amateur affair run for club members.

Léon Houa won in ten hours, forty-eight minutes, averaging little more than 23 kilometres an hour, and he went on to win the next two editions as well. The race lapsed for years at a time in its early decades before settling into the fixture now ranked alongside Milan-San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix and the Tour of Lombardy as one of cycling's five Monuments.

Bobby Jones built Augusta National as a retreat from competition, not a stage for it, and the first tournament there in 1934 was called the Augusta National Invitation; Jones himself insisted on the modest name and only agreed to Masters later, when the press had already made it stick.

Horton Smith won that inaugural event by a single stroke, holing a birdie putt on the 17th to take the lead for good. Jones, lured out of retirement to play his own course, tied for 13th. The tournament became one of golf's four majors and has been played at Augusta every year since.

The often-told story has Archer's trainer walking the horse more than 700 kilometres from Nowra to Melbourne to make the race. Newspaper shipping records from the time show otherwise: Archer travelled from New South Wales by steamer, the SS City of Sydney, along with several other runners.

He won regardless, and comfortably enough that his rivals' owners petitioned to have his entry to the following year's Cup refused, unsuccessfully; Archer won that one too. The Flemington race he opened has grown into the fixture that stops Australia each November, but the walking legend, kept alive partly by a 1985 film, has no basis in the shipping news of 1861.

Cycling's oldest Monument began in April 1907 as a race almost nobody entered: only 33 riders started the roughly 288 kilometre route from Milan to the Ligurian coast, put together by La Gazzetta dello Sport to promote the paper rather than to crown a champion of anything in particular.

Lucien Petit-Breton, a Frenchman racing under a name he adopted after his family emigrated to Argentina, won the inaugural edition. The race survived poor early turnout to become one of cycling's five Monuments, run every spring since with only wartime interruptions.

The race almost belonged to Mercedes. Rudolf Caracciola's supercharged 7-litre car overtook William Grover-Williams on lap 36 of the 100-lap race around Monte Carlo, only for the smaller, more fuel-efficient Bugatti to retake the lead after the pit stops and pull away by more than a lap.

Grover-Williams, a British driver racing in what became known as Bugatti's British racing green, won the first Monaco Grand Prix on 14 April 1929. He later worked for Britain's Special Operations Executive during the Second World War and was captured and killed by the Gestapo.

The first Monte Carlo Rally in January 1911 was not a race to a finish line so much as a test of endurance from wherever a driver started. Twenty-three cars set out from eleven different European cities, converging on Monaco, with Henri Rougier's group driving roughly 1,020 kilometres from Paris.

Rougier won in a Turcat-Mery, but the result was decided as much by judging as by driving: cars were scored on the elegance of their arrival, passenger comfort and condition, not simply on time or distance. Complaints about that scoring did nothing to change the outcome, and Rougier kept the title of first winner.

The vehicle that crossed the line first at Rouen was not declared the winner. Count Albert de Dion's steam tractor led the whole way and finished in six hours and forty-eight minutes, but the judges ruled it ineligible because it needed a stoker riding alongside, breaking a contest rule about vehicles a single person could operate.

Le Petit Journal had billed the event, run from Paris on 22 July 1894, as a trial of horseless carriages rather than a race, and the prize was split between Panhard et Levassor and Peugeot, whose petrol cars met the rules de Dion's did not. The contest still counts as the first competitive motoring event, one won on a technicality rather than by whoever got there fastest.

The Fédération Internationale de Motocyclisme ran its first world championship season in 1949, six classes deep, before Formula One had held a single world championship race. Leslie Graham took the premier 500cc title on an AJS, riding a machine built by a small English firm rather than one of the Italian factories that would soon dominate the class.

The calendar that year was thin by modern standards, just a handful of grands prix across Europe including the Isle of Man TT, already decades old by 1949 and folded straight into the new championship's points table. Motorcycle racing's world title predates every other motorsport championship still running, F1 included, by a full year.

Only eight teams entered, and the NCAA itself barely wanted the job: the tournament ran at a loss and the college association nearly handed the whole idea back to a coaches group after year one. Oregon, built around a frontline nicknamed the Tall Firs, beat Ohio State 46 to 33 in the final at Patten Gymnasium in Evanston, Illinois, on 27 March 1939.

The bigger draw that season was still the NIT in New York, which had started a year earlier and kept more prestige for another decade. Oregon's win produced no bracket, no office pools and barely any national coverage; the tournament's now-familiar name and scale came later, once television made a one-loss-and-out format worth broadcasting coast to coast.

Jim Thorpe won the first Olympic decathlon at Stockholm in 1912 by a wide margin, and his points total was a benchmark for years, but the medal did not stay his for long. Within months, reports surfaced that he had been paid to play minor league baseball, breaching strict amateur rules, and the IOC stripped his titles in 1913.

Thorpe had not hidden the payments, which were modest and common among college athletes at the time playing under assumed names. The IOC did not restore his records and medals until 1982, decades after his death, by which time the decathlon itself had long been contested under far looser amateur rules.

No ancient Olympics ever carried a torch between cities; the relay is a modern invention, devised for the 1936 Berlin Games by organising committee official Carl Diem and enthusiastically backed by the Nazi government for the propaganda value of an unbroken line running from ancient Greece to the Third Reich.

A flame was lit by the sun's rays at Olympia and carried by more than 3,000 runners across Greece, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Hungary, Austria and Czechoslovakia before reaching Berlin's stadium. Every Games since has repeated the relay, stripped of the original politics but keeping the theatre.

The first One Day International happened by accident. Rain wiped out the first three days of the third Ashes Test at Melbourne in January 1971, leaving no way to finish a five-day match, so administrators arranged a one-off 40-over-a-side game on the scheduled final day instead, largely to give ticket holders something for their money.

Australia beat England by five wickets in front of about 46,000 spectators, a crowd far larger than a struggling Test match would likely have drawn. The format's popularity that day helped push cricket toward the limited-overs game as a fixture in its own right, and the first Cricket World Cup followed just four years later, in 1975.

Only eight golfers entered the first Open at Prestwick in 1860, and entry was restricted to professionals, making the event less open than its later name suggests; amateurs were not allowed in until the following year. Three rounds of Prestwick's twelve holes were played in a single day.

Willie Park Sr beat Tom Morris Sr by two strokes to take the Challenge Belt, a leather trophy rather than a trophy claret jug, which was not introduced until decades later. Park and Morris between them dominated the Open's first years, and their rivalry gave the young championship its first sustained storyline.

The challenge came from Cambridge, issued by a Cambridge student to a Harrow schoolfriend now at Oxford, and the crews rowed roughly two and a quarter miles from Hambleden Lock to Henley Bridge rather than the Putney to Mortlake course used today. Oxford wore dark blue, Cambridge white with pink sashes, and an estimated 20,000 people turned out to watch.

Oxford won easily in 14 minutes 30 seconds, and the fixture did not become annual straight away; the second race waited until 1836. It settled into a yearly event on the Thames tideway from 1856, and the dark blue versus light blue rivalry that started at Henley in 1829 has continued with only wartime gaps ever since.

Antonio Scaino was a priest and scholar, not a player of note, when he wrote his 1555 treatise on ball games.
