In it he wrote down, for the first time, how the arm-guard ball game pallone col bracciale should be played, a sport contested by striking an inflated leather ball with a wooden guard strapped over the forearm. His book also covered tennis and other ball games, treating them as worthy of the same serious analysis as classical texts.

Pallone was popular across northern Italy for centuries, played in long rectangular courts with spectators lining both sides, and it survived into the twentieth century as a betting sport before television and football pushed it into obscurity. Scaino's treatise remains the earliest known attempt to write rules down rather than leave them to local custom.

The Pan American Games had actually been planned for 1942, drawn up alongside the 1937 Pan American Congress that founded the idea, but the Second World War forced a decade's delay. Buenos Aires finally hosted the opening edition in 1951, gathering more than 2,500 athletes from 21 nations across the Americas, from the United States and Canada down through the Caribbean and South America.

Argentina used the Games as a political display under Juan Peron's government, building facilities and staging an opening ceremony meant to project the country's standing in the hemisphere. The event has run every four years since, always in the year before the Olympics, giving American nations a dedicated continental championship distinct from the Olympic programme.

Two textile mill owners in Roubaix built the town's velodrome and needed something to fill it, so they sponsored a race from Paris to draw a crowd for the opening. Held on 19 April 1896, it drew riders including Maurice Garin, who would later win the first Tour de France, finishing third here.

Josef Fischer, a German rider, won in nine hours and seventeen minutes over roads that were already rough, though the punishing cobbles that define the modern race came later, laid by industrial towns for carts rather than for cyclists. Fischer's 1,000 franc prize was a serious sum, and the race has run most years since.

The PGA of America was founded in January 1916, largely through the backing of department store owner Rodman Wanamaker, who wanted a national organisation for club professionals and put up funding for a championship trophy the same year. The first PGA Championship followed that October at Siwanoy Country Club in New York.

Jim Barnes, an English-born professional who had emigrated to the United States, won the match-play final and took home 500 dollars along with the Wanamaker Trophy, the same trophy still awarded to PGA Championship winners today. The event stayed match play for decades before switching to stroke play in 1958.

The Ryder Cup only pitted the United States against Europe, leaving strong golfing nations such as Australia and South Africa without an equivalent international stage. The PGA Tour created the Presidents Cup to fill that gap, first played in September 1994 at Robert Trent Jones Golf Club in Gainesville, Virginia, with former President Gerald Ford serving as honorary chairman.

Hale Irwin's United States team beat David Graham's International squad, drawn from non-European countries, by a score of 20 to 12. Greg Norman, ranked second on the International side, withdrew days before the event through illness and was replaced by Bradley Hughes. The event has been held roughly every two years since, usually alternating hosts.

The race run at Longchamp on 3 October 1920 was not conceived as a one-off novelty but as a peace-time successor to France's wartime racing calendar, named for the monument rather than any military victory. Comrade, a three-year-old colt owned by Evremond de Saint-Alary, won the inaugural running and its 150,000-franc purse.

The distance, roughly 2,400 metres, and the autumn date have barely changed since. What did change was the field: within a few decades the Arc drew the best middle-distance horses from across Europe rather than mostly French entries, turning a domestic prize into the continent's benchmark end-of-season race.

The first professional road world championship, held at the new Nurburgring circuit on 21 July 1927, covered about 182 kilometres around the Adenau area rather than a city circuit. Alfredo Binda attacked on the second-to-last lap and finished more than seven minutes clear of the field.

Costante Girardengo and Domenico Piemontesi filled out an all-Italian podium behind him. Binda's win earned him the first rainbow-striped jersey awarded to a world champion, a design still used today, and he went on to take the title twice more while also winning the Giro d'Italia five times.

The medieval joust as popular imagination pictures it, two knights charging with lances in a fenced arena, is not what the word originally described. Its first known appearance is in a peace charter Count Baldwin III of Hainaut issued for the town of Valenciennes in 1114, which orders local peacekeepers to avoid leaving town to attend javelin sports, tournaments and similar gatherings.

Early tournaments were closer to mock battles, mounted groups charging across open countryside with real weapons, and injuries and deaths were common enough that the Church periodically tried to ban the practice outright. The single-combat joust with blunted lances and safety barriers only developed over the following two centuries out of these rougher, deadlier group melees.

Rhythmic gymnastics grew out of Soviet and Eastern Bloc physical culture programmes that blended dance, ballet and apparatus work, and it took decades before the International Gymnastics Federation recognised it as a discipline separate from artistic gymnastics with rings, bars and vaults.

The first World Championships were held in Budapest in 1963, contested only as an individual all-around event rather than the team and group formats added later. Soviet gymnast Ludmila Savinkova won the inaugural title, opening a period of Soviet and Bulgarian dominance that the sport did not shake until well after the Cold War ended.

The match at Raeburn Place on 27 March 1871 came about because Scottish clubs, tired of English newspapers ignoring rugby north of the border, challenged England directly through the press. Twenty players a side took the field, more than double a modern team, under rules only just settled by the new Rugby Football Union.

Scotland scored a try and converted goal to win by a scoreline recorded as one goal to one try, since points values had not yet been standardised. The fixture became annual, and the Scotland-England match is still the oldest international rivalry in rugby union.

Rugby union's own administrators had resisted a World Cup for years, worried that a global tournament would push the amateur sport toward professionalism. New Zealand and Australia jointly hosted the first one in 1987 once the International Rugby Board finally agreed, with sixteen teams competing across the two countries.

The hosts beat France 29-9 in the final at Eden Park in Auckland, with All Black wing John Kirwan scoring a try remembered for beating half of France's defence alone on a run from deep in his own half. The tournament drew modest crowds compared with later editions, but set the format the sport still uses.

The rules were not written for golf in general but for one competition: a silver club offered by the City of Edinburgh, open to any golfer who cared to enter, played over five holes on Leith Links. The Gentlemen Golfers needed a shared code only because outsiders, not just their own members, would be teeing off.

Thirteen short articles cover the essentials still recognisable today, including playing the ball as it lies and the order of holing out, but say nothing about a standard number of holes or a fixed course length, both left to whatever ground a club happened to play. The Gentlemen Golfers later moved to Muirfield and became the Honourable Company of Edinburgh Golfers.

Samuel Ryder, a seed merchant who made his fortune selling penny packets of seeds by mail, funded the trophy and gave his name to the contest after watching British and American professionals play informal matches earlier in the decade. Walter Hagen captained the United States team at Worcester Country Club in Massachusetts for the first official match in 1927.

The Americans won comfortably, 9.5 to 2.5, a lopsided start to what became a fiercely competitive biennial fixture. Play alternated between American and British soil in the following decades, and the format later expanded to include continental European players once Britain and Ireland alone could no longer keep the matches close.

Golf's Ryder Cup had run for men since 1927 with nothing equivalent for women until insurance executive Karsten Solheim, whose company sponsored several LPGA players, put his name and money behind a matching event. The first edition was played at Lake Nona Golf and Country Club in Orlando, Florida, from 16 to 18 November 1990, Europe against the United States.

Kathy Whitworth captained a US side that included Betsy King and Beth Daniel to an 11.5 to 4.5 victory over Mickey Walker's European team. The format borrowed the Ryder Cup's foursomes, four ball and singles structure directly. It has been held every two years since, alternating hosts between the two continents.

Squash had no single recognised individual world championship until 1976, despite decades of national titles and informal claims to being the best player alive. The International Squash Rackets Federation organised the first World Open that year in London to settle the question with a proper tournament draw.

Geoff Hunt, an Australian who had already dominated the amateur game, won the inaugural title. The World Open has been held most years since and is now widely treated as squash's most prestigious individual event, alongside the British Open, which predates it but carries less claim to a truly global field.

The race was not called the St Leger when it was first run at Doncaster. It began as a sweepstake organised by Anthony St Leger, a local army officer and MP, and only took his name two years later once it had become an established fixture on the town's course.

It predates the Epsom Derby by three years and the Epsom Oaks by two, making it the oldest of the five races that make up the English Classics. Run over a demanding one mile and six furlongs, longer than the other Classics, it was designed as a test of stamina in horses bred for speed over shorter distances.

Before 1980, interstate rugby league in Australia was decided by where a player currently held his club contract, which meant Queenslanders who had moved to Sydney clubs were forced to represent New South Wales against their home state. Queensland officials pushed for a change so players would instead represent the state they were originally from.

The first game under the new rule was played at Lang Park in Brisbane on 7 July 1980, and Queensland won 20-10 behind captain Arthur Beetson, who had crossed to play for his birth state against the club he represented in Sydney. The result convinced administrators to make origin selection permanent, and the concept grew into the annual State of Origin series.

Ludwig Guttmann ran the spinal injuries unit at Stoke Mandeville Hospital and did not think of sport as therapy alone; he timed it deliberately to land on the opening day of the London Olympics, 29 July 1948. Sixteen injured servicemen and women, all in wheelchairs, competed in archery on the hospital lawn while the actual Games opened a short train ride away.

Guttmann kept running the event every year afterwards, and it grew: Dutch competitors joined in 1952, and by 1960 the Games had moved to Rome to run alongside the Olympics there, the gathering now counted as the first Paralympics. Archery, the sport chosen because many of Guttmann's patients had upper-body strength but no use of their legs, remained on the programme from that first afternoon onward.

Steve Davis potted all fifteen reds with the black and cleared the colours at the 1982 Lada Classic in Oldham, the first maximum break of 147 ever shown live on television. The sponsor's prize was one of the Lada cars it made, handed over for a feat that had happened before, but never with cameras present to record it.

Snooker's television audience had grown quickly through the late 1970s once colour sets made the game watchable at home, and a maximum break needed cameras present to count as a public event rather than a claim. Davis was already the leading player of his generation, and the decade that followed belonged largely to him.

Only about a thousand television sets existed in the New York area capable of picking up the signal on 22 October 1939, so NBC's broadcast of the Brooklyn Dodgers hosting the Philadelphia Eagles at Ebbets Field reached almost nobody watching, even as roughly 13,000 fans filled the stands in person.

One announcer, Skip Walz, called the game using two cameras, one fixed and one that could pan the field. The Dodgers won 23-14. Regular network television coverage of the NFL did not begin until 1951, but this experimental broadcast is recognised as the game that started it.

The winners were not Malaysia, a country that did not yet exist. In 1949 the team was Malaya, and it beat Denmark eight matches to one over two days at the Queens Hall in Preston, England, to take the trophy donated by former English player George Thomas. Malaya's biggest name, Wong Peng Soon, missed the final through injury and the team won it without him.

Thomas had proposed the competition years earlier, and had a solid silver cup made and ready long before enough countries agreed to enter; the Second World War delayed the first contest by most of a decade. Malaya's win opened a run of Asian dominance that has barely loosened since: a non-Asian side has not held the men's team trophy in more than seventy years.

Test cricket had run for 83 years and nearly 500 matches without a single tie before the Gabba in December 1960. Australia needed six runs off the final over with three wickets left, and the last few balls swung between a West Indies win, an Australian win and a tie in the space of minutes.

Off the final ball, Ian Meckiff and Lindsay Kline attempted a suicidal single. Fieldsman Joe Solomon, throwing from square leg, hit the stumps directly to run Meckiff out and level the scores exactly. West Indies captain Frank Worrell, the first black man to lead the side for a full series, later called the match cricket's finest advertisement.

Twenty20 was not invented to test cricket's limits, it was invented to sell tickets to people who had given up on the county game. The England and Wales Cricket Board designed a twenty-over format with cheerleaders and fireworks specifically to draw a crowd that one-day cricket had stopped reaching.

The Rose Bowl hosted the format's first official match on 13 June 2003, Hampshire beating Sussex in front of a crowd well beyond what county cricket usually drew. The Twenty20 Cup that followed proved popular enough at the gate that the format spread within a few years to national boards worldwide and eventually produced the IPL.

Betty Uber, herself a former English badminton champion, had spent years lobbying for a women's equivalent of the Thomas Cup before the sport's governing body agreed. She donated the trophy and gave it her own name, and the inaugural final was staged at Lytham St Annes in England in March 1957.

The United States, led by Judy Devlin and her sister Susan, beat Denmark 6-1 in the final after eliminating India 7-0 in the semis. It began a run of American dominance in women's team badminton that lasted until the sport's centre of gravity shifted decisively to Asia in the following decades.

UFC 1 was staged in Denver on 12 November 1993 as an eight-man single-night tournament pitting fighters from different disciplines, boxing, sumo, karate, kickboxing, against each other with almost no restrictions beyond eye gouging and biting. Organisers billed it as a way to settle which style actually worked against another under real conditions.

Royce Gracie, a slight 175-pound Brazilian jiu-jitsu practitioner, won all three of his fights that night by submission against larger opponents, including a 26-second win over a 400 pound sumo wrestler in the opening round. His performance is widely credited with proving that ground grappling could beat size and striking, and it shaped what mixed martial arts training would become.

The United States National Lawn Tennis Association held its first championship in Newport, Rhode Island in August 1881, only three years after the sport had reached America from England. Richard Sears, a Harvard student, won the men's singles title and then defended it every year until he retired unbeaten in 1887.

The tournament stayed at Newport for over three decades before moving to Forest Hills in New York in 1915, and later to Flushing Meadows. Renamed the US Open once professionals were admitted in 1968, it traces its lineage directly back to that first Newport meeting.

Only eleven players started the first U.S. Open, held on 4 October 1895 on a nine-hole course in Newport, Rhode Island, played four times round in a single day. It was tacked onto the end of the U.S. Amateur championship almost as an afterthought, without the prestige the title now carries.

Horace Rawlins, a twenty-one-year-old English professional working at Newport, shot 173 over the four loops to beat Willie Dunn by two strokes and take home 150 dollars and a gold medal. The USGA has run the championship every year since bar wartime gaps, making it the oldest of American golf's national opens.

Thirteen sailors set out from Les Sables d'Olonne in November 1989 for a race with no support crews, no stops and no help of any kind: sail the world alone or retire. Only seven finished. The idea, born from French singlehanded ocean racing, was to strip away every safety net the sport usually allowed and see who came back.

Titouan Lamazou crossed the line first on 16 March 1990, after 109 days, 8 hours and 49 minutes at sea aboard his monohull Ecureuil d'Aquitaine II. Loick Peyron finished less than a day behind him. The race has run roughly every four years since, and finishers now routinely beat Lamazou's time by weeks thanks to faster hulls and better routing.

Spain's national sports newspaper Informaciones organised the first Vuelta a Espana in 1935, following the pattern already set by the Tour de France and the Giro d'Italia, both decades older. Fifty riders started a race run over 14 stages and roughly 3,400 kilometres, finishing back in Madrid.

The Belgian Gustaaf Deloor won, beating his own brother Alfons into second place overall; Gustaaf returned to defend the title successfully in 1936. The Spanish Civil War then broke out that July, and the Vuelta did not run again until 1941.

The first Walker Cup was played on 28 and 29 August 1922 at the National Golf Links of America in Southampton, New York, four 36-hole foursomes followed by eight singles, each of the twelve matches worth a single point. It was named for George Herbert Walker, a United States Golf Association president and, decades later, great-grandfather of a US president.

The United States won 8 to 4, and home advantage mattered more than the scoreline suggests: American amateurs had access to warmer weather and more courses than their British and Irish counterparts. The format has been tweaked since, but the biennial rhythm and the amateur-only entry rule set in 1922 still hold.

Women were barred from Olympic distance running for decades on the claim that a marathon was too taxing for female athletes, a view the International Olympic Committee only abandoned for the 1984 Los Angeles Games. Joan Benoit of the United States broke away after three miles and ran alone for the rest of the race.

Benoit had undergone knee surgery only seventeen days before the US Olympic trials that qualified her, an operation that would ordinarily have ended a season. She finished the Los Angeles course in 2:24:52, well clear of Norway's Grete Waitz, and the gap she opened early was never seriously threatened.

FIFA had resisted a women's championship for decades, and the 1991 tournament in China was staged carefully under a different name, the World Championship for Women's Football, with a smaller ball and shortened halves rather than the men's rules. It was only retroactively folded into the Women's World Cup lineage once the event proved itself.

Michelle Akers scored twice as the Americans won the final 2-1 in Guangzhou, a result built on a team drawing on college soccer programmes that Norway and other European sides did not yet have. The tournament drew crowds far larger than organisers had planned for, including a reported 65,000 at the opening match.

Swimming, diving and water polo had been contested at the Olympics for decades, but never in a standalone world championship of their own until 1973, when the sport's governing body organised one in Belgrade, then part of Yugoslavia. Synchronised swimming was included as well, making it a broader gathering than any single Olympic swim programme.

Athletes from 47 countries competed, filling a gap between Olympic cycles and giving swimmers a major title to chase in years without the Games. The event has been held roughly every two to four years since, and eventually absorbed open water swimming and masters events, growing into what is now known as the World Aquatics Championships.

Only four skaters entered the event the International Skating Union sanctioned as its first world championship, held on 9 February 1896 in Saint Petersburg. There was no women's category at all; competitors were judged on compulsory figures, tracing set patterns into the ice, and on free skating, the two disciplines that still make up the sport.

Gilbert Fuchs of Germany won, ahead of Austria's Gustav Hugel and the American-born Georg Sanders, who lived in Russia. Fuchs recaptured the world title a decade later in Munich in 1906. The championship itself grew from that single small contest in Russia into the sport's principal annual event, held nearly every year since.

The event held in London in December 1926 was originally billed as a European championship, and only became recognised as the first World Championships once the International Table Tennis Federation was formally constituted around the same gathering. Hungary dominated the early men's and women's titles that emerged from it.

The sport itself had circulated under various trade names, including Ping-Pong, for decades before this event gave it a governed, standardised competition structure. That 1926 meeting fixed the rules, equipment standards and championship format that let the game spread as an organised sport rather than a parlour pastime.

William Fitzstephen wrote his account of London as a preface to a biography of Thomas Becket, not as sports history, which is why it survives at all. He describes older boys carrying a large ball into open fields after dinner on Shrove Tuesday, watched by crowds of men, elders and fathers on horseback who came to see the young play out their own vigour.

No pitch, no goals and no rules are given, and the game he describes is closer to a scramble than anything a modern fan would recognise as football. It matters because it is the earliest surviving English text to put a ball game and London youths in the same sentence, giving every later mob-football ban something concrete to point back to.

Florence Griffith-Joyner ran 10.49 seconds in the 100 metres at the US Olympic trials in Indianapolis on 16 July 1988, cutting almost three tenths of a second off the existing world record in a single race. The wind gauge for her heat read a legal 0.0 metres per second, even though the concurrent triple jump recorded a tailwind well above the allowed limit.

The reading has been disputed ever since on the suspicion the gauge malfunctioned, but World Athletics has never annulled it, and it remains the official world record decades later. Griffith-Joyner, known for painted nails and one-legged racing suits, went on to win three gold medals at the Seoul Olympics weeks afterward.

William McGregor, a director at Aston Villa, grew tired of clubs arranging their own friendly fixtures with no guaranteed income from match to match. In March 1888 he wrote to several clubs proposing a fixed league with a set schedule, and representatives met in Manchester to agree it.

Twelve clubs, all from the Midlands and the north of England, formed the Football League that April, the first organised league competition in world football. Preston North End won the inaugural 1888-89 season unbeaten, and the league structure McGregor proposed became the template every football league since has copied.

Ford staged the finish it wanted, not the one the rules allowed. Team management asked leader Ken Miles to slow so all three GT40s crossed together for a photograph, handing what looked like a shared victory to Miles and Bruce McLaren's crew. Officials ruled that McLaren's car had covered more distance, since it started eight metres behind Miles on the grid, and awarded him the win outright.

Miles never got a chance to contest the decision. He died three months later testing a Ford GT40 Mark IV at the same Le Mans circuit. The 1-2-3 finish itself stood: it ended a run of Ferrari victories at Le Mans and gave an American manufacturer its first overall win there, a result Ford had built the GT40 programme specifically to achieve.

College football nearly did not survive to 1906. Mass-formation plays like the flying wedge packed runners behind a wall of blockers, and the resulting pile-ups killed at least 18 players in the 1905 season alone, prompting President Theodore Roosevelt to press the sport's leaders to reform the game or see it banned.

A rules committee responded by legalising the forward pass, requiring a neutral zone between the lines, and setting a minimum of six men on the offensive line. The pass was hedged with restrictions, including a five-yard penalty for an incomplete one, so it spread slowly rather than transforming the sport overnight.

Dick Fosbury did not invent his back-first clearance to win in Mexico City; he had been jumping that way since high school, after struggling with the straddle technique his coaches taught. Commentators at the 1968 Games mocked the style as ungainly, and several rival coaches predicted it would injure whoever tried to copy it at speed.

Fosbury cleared 2.24 metres for gold, an Olympic record, landing on foam pits that had only recently replaced sawdust and made the head-first fall survivable. Within a decade the flop had replaced the straddle at the top level almost entirely; by the 1980 Olympics nearly every finalist used some version of it.

The Home Nations Championship had run as a purely British and Irish affair since the 1880s before France was invited in for the 1910 season, turning it into the Five Nations. France's own rugby union had only recently organised itself into a body capable of fielding a recognised national side.

France lost all four matches in that first campaign, and it took until the 1950s for the side to win the title outright. The tournament kept the Five Nations name until Italy joined in 2000, when it became the Six Nations still played today.

Trained by Henry Cecil and ridden mostly by Tom Queally, Frankel never lost a race across three seasons, winning his fourteen starts by a combined margin that regularly left the rest of the field labouring. His trainer, fighting cancer through much of that run, called him the best horse he had ever handled.

His final start, the 2012 Champion Stakes at Ascot, was also Cecil's last big winner before he died the following year. Frankel retired to stud with an official rating higher than any horse Timeform had assessed, and his unbeaten record made him one of the very few champions retired purely on reputation rather than a loss forcing the decision.

Dawn Fraser had already won consecutive Olympic golds in the 100 metres freestyle before she chased the one-minute barrier itself, a mark that carried the same weight in swimming that the four-minute mile carried in athletics.

On 27 October 1962 in Melbourne, Fraser swam 59.9 seconds to become the first woman under a minute for the distance. She went on to win the event at a third Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, the first swimmer of either sex to win the same individual event three times, before a car crash and a suspension pushed her toward retirement.

Gichin Funakoshi was 54 and largely unknown outside Okinawa when he demonstrated karate-jutsu at a Ministry of Education physical education exhibition in Tokyo in 1922. Judo's founder, Jigoro Kano, saw it and invited Funakoshi to give a further demonstration at the Kodokan, judo's own headquarters dojo.

More than 300 people, including newspaper reporters, packed the Kodokan for that second showing. The reception persuaded Funakoshi to stay in Tokyo rather than return home, and he began teaching at a dormitory for Okinawan students, work that grew into the Shotokan style still practised worldwide.

Irish athletics before 1884 was run largely by English-controlled bodies that favoured cricket, rugby and athletics meetings held under rules that shut out working-class competitors. Michael Cusack, a teacher and hurling enthusiast, called a meeting at Hayes' Hotel in Thurles that November to set up an Irish alternative.

Seven men attended, and they founded the Gaelic Athletic Association to codify and promote hurling and Gaelic football rather than let them fade under English-run sport. The GAA grew into a mass amateur movement, and its All-Ireland finals still fill Croke Park each September.

The Barbarians, a club with no home ground that assembles star players for one-off matches, faced the touring All Blacks at Cardiff Arms Park in January 1973. The move began deep in the Barbarians' own half after Phil Bennett sidestepped three defenders near his own line, an act of defiance rather than caution.

The ball passed through the hands of JPR Williams, John Pullin, John Dawes and others across the width of the pitch before Gareth Edwards, sprinting from scrum half, dived to finish in the corner. Commentator Cliff Morgan's excited call of the try has been replayed almost as often as the score itself. It is routinely voted the greatest try rugby has produced.

The granite stele does not honour a battle. It records a shot: at an assembly of Mongol nobles held after the conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire, Genghis Khan's nephew Yesungge sent an arrow to a mark measured at 335 alds, roughly 536 metres, and the feat was thought worth carving in stone.

The inscription is the oldest surviving text written in the Mongolian script, which the empire had only just adopted from a captured Uyghur scribe. It was found in the 1800s near the Kherlen river and moved to St Petersburg, where it still sits in the Hermitage rather than in Mongolia.

Alan Shepard smuggled the equipment himself, taping a six-iron head to a lunar sample-collection handle and stashing a couple of golf balls in a spare sock aboard Apollo 14 in February 1971. NASA had not sanctioned the stunt, and Shepard, the first American in space eight years earlier, kept it quiet until he was already standing on the Moon.

Wearing a stiff pressurised suit and swinging with one gloved hand, Shepard mostly missed on his first attempt, then connected on his second and third. He later claimed the ball travelled miles in the Moon's weak gravity and thin exosphere; footage instead suggests a modest shot of perhaps 20 to 40 metres, still the first golf ball ever struck off Earth.

Steffi Graf won the Australian, French, Wimbledon and US Opens in 1988, then added Olympic singles gold in Seoul that same year when tennis returned to the Games after a 64-year absence. No man or woman has completed all five since, which is why the term Golden Slam exists specifically to describe what Graf alone has done.

She was 19 when the run began and lost only three sets across the four majors that year, a margin that made her season look inevitable in hindsight despite Martina Navratilova still being ranked ahead of her at the start of it. Graf's calendar Grand Slam alone would have been rare; adding the Olympics made 1988 unrepeated.

At 168 metres long, the Great Ballcourt the Maya dedicated at Chichen Itza around 864 dwarfs every other ballcourt found in Mesoamerica, more than double the length of most contemporary examples. Stone rings set high on the side walls, carved relief panels showing decapitation, and a temple perched at one end all suggest the games played there carried ceremonial weight beyond simple competition.

The rubber ball used in the Mesoamerican game could weigh several kilograms and was struck only with the hips, thighs or shoulders, never the hands or feet, making scoring through the elevated rings an unusual feat. Chichen Itza's court sat at the centre of a Maya city that dominated the Yucatan for centuries, and its scale reflects a game bound up with political and religious authority, not casual sport.

The row was over money, not tactics. Rugby's governing body insisted the game stay strictly amateur, but factory workers in the industrial north could not afford to lose a Saturday's wages to play unpaid, and clubs there had been quietly compensating them for lost time. On 12 August 1895 the Rugby Football Union threatened suspension for any club caught doing it.

Representatives of twenty-one clubs met at the George Hotel in Huddersfield on 29 August and resigned from the RFU en masse, forming the Northern Rugby Football Union to legalise those payments. The split did not touch the rules of play at first, only who could be paid; the two codes only diverged into the different game rugby league is today over the following years.

The 1958 NFL Championship at Yankee Stadium was tied 17-17 with seven seconds left when Baltimore's Steve Myhra kicked a field goal to force the first sudden-death overtime in league history. Television carried the game nationally, and pro football had never before held that large an audience for a single match.

In overtime the Giants went three and out, helped by a Frank Gifford run ruled inches short of a first down, and Johnny Unitas drove the Colts downfield for a touchdown to win 23-17. The game is widely credited with turning American professional football into a television sport rather than a regional one.

Wayne Gretzky scored his 50th goal in the Edmonton Oilers' 39th game of the 1981-82 season, a pace nobody before him had come close to touching. He finished with 92 goals and 212 points in that season, both marks that stood alone for decades and neither has been matched since.

Gretzky was 21, slight for a hockey player, and had been dismissed by some scouts as too small to dominate professionally. His 92 goals came from reading the ice rather than raw speed or size, a style that made him hard to defend against because he was rarely where the play seemed to be heading.

There was no pool for the swimming events at the first modern Olympics. Competitors were taken out into the open, cold waters of the Bay of Zea near Piraeus and started from small boats, in water around 13 degrees Celsius with waves reported at four metres. Alfred Hajos, an eighteen-year-old Hungarian, was among those who had to swim it regardless.

Hajos won the 100 metre freestyle in one minute twenty two seconds, the first individual swimming title of the Olympic era, and added the 1200 metre freestyle days later in just over eighteen minutes. In 1924 he returned to the Games as an architect and won a silver medal in the art competitions for a stadium design, a category since dropped from the Olympics.

Hank Aaron spent the winter before 1974 receiving death threats and racist mail over his pursuit of Babe Ruth's career home run record of 714, a number many Americans regarded as untouchable. He tied Ruth on his first swing of the season, then homered again four days later, on 8 April 1974 in Atlanta, off Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Al Downing.

Two fans ran onto the field to join him rounding the bases, an intrusion the broadcast caught live. Aaron finished his career with 755 home runs, a total that no one beat for 33 years until Barry Bonds passed it in 2007. Aaron never sought that kind of hostility again and later said the chase had cost him part of the joy of the game.

Abe Saperstein put the team together in Chicago in 1926, not Harlem, taking the name because Harlem was already synonymous with Black basketball talent and Globetrotters because he intended to tour rather than play a fixed home schedule. The early team barnstormed small Midwestern towns, often playing on dance-hall floors rather than proper courts.

Comedy routines were folded into games gradually, as a way to keep lopsided scorelines entertaining for paying crowds, not part of the original concept. Decades of exhibition tours against club and college teams turned the Globetrotters into one of the most travelled sports franchises in the world, still performing more than 90 years later.

Henry II was jousting to celebrate two royal weddings when his opponent's lance shattered on his breastplate and a splinter drove up through the visor of his helmet, into his eye and skull. He lingered for ten days before dying, attended by the royal physician and, according to later legend, by Ambroise Pare, who tested treatments on the severed heads of executed criminals to understand the wound.

The joust had already been a bad omen: Henry had insisted on a second run against the same opponent, Gabriel de Montgomery, despite his wife Catherine de' Medici's reported unease. His death left the French throne to a line of young, short-reigned sons and helped tip the country toward the Wars of Religion that followed within a few years.

Ben Hogan entered only six competitive tournaments in 1953, still recovering strength lost in a near-fatal car crash four years earlier that had crushed his pelvis and left doctors doubting he would walk again, let alone play golf. He won five of the six, including the Masters, the U.S. Open, and, on his only trip to Britain, the Open Championship at Carnoustie.

The three wins are now called the Hogan Slam, though the term was coined later; no one used it in 1953. He could not attempt the fourth major, the PGA Championship, because its match-play format that year overlapped with his travel to Scotland, leaving the modern calendar Grand Slam permanently out of reach for him despite the rest of the season.

England had never lost a home match to a team from outside the British Isles before 25 November 1953, a run stretching back to the 1870s. Hungary's forwards, arranged in a deep-lying centre-forward system England's defenders had no answer for, went 4-1 up before half time at Wembley and won 6 to 3, with Ferenc Puskas scoring twice.

One moment stood out even within the scoreline: Puskas dragged the ball back with the sole of his boot past a lunging Billy Wright, who was left tackling empty air, before scoring. English football spent years afterward reassessing its tactics and coaching methods in response, a reckoning the press at the time called, without much exaggeration, a national humiliation.

Athletics had no single rulebook before 1912: national federations recognised different world records and disagreed over amateur eligibility, which made comparing performances between countries close to meaningless. Delegates from 17 national federations met in Stockholm right after that year's Olympics to fix this by founding the IAAF.

The new body's first task was to standardise record-keeping and define amateurism uniformly, a rule that later cost Jim Thorpe his own Stockholm medals. The federation has changed its name more than once since, most recently to World Athletics, but it remains the sport's sole global authority on records and rules.

Lambeau Field's electric heating coils failed overnight before kickoff, and the temperature at game time read minus 13 Fahrenheit, with a wind chill estimated near minus 48. The 1967 NFL Championship between Green Bay and Dallas is remembered as the coldest game in league history, cold enough that referee Norm Schachter's whistle reportedly froze to his lip.

Green Bay trailed 17-14 with sixteen seconds left when quarterback Bart Starr, out of timeouts, chose to run the ball himself rather than risk a pass or a slick field-goal snap. He followed guard Jerry Kramer's block through the middle for the winning score. The Packers' third straight NFL title sent Vince Lombardi's team to Super Bowl II, which they also won.

Ice hockey's international federation was founded in Paris in 1908 by delegates from Belgium, France, Great Britain and Switzerland, four countries not otherwise associated with the sport's later powerhouses. Canada, where the modern game had been codified decades earlier, was not among the founders.

The body was named the Ligue Internationale de Hockey sur Glace before adopting its current English initials, IIHF, later on. It set out to standardise rules across Europe for a sport that had spread from Canadian universities to European rinks mostly through students and travelling clubs.

With 22 seconds left and Pittsburgh trailing Oakland 7-6 in the 1972 AFC playoffs, Terry Bradshaw threw toward Frenchy Fuqua on fourth down. Raiders safety Jack Tatum hit Fuqua as the ball arrived, and it flew backward. Rookie Franco Harris scooped it off his shoetops before it hit the turf and ran 43 yards for the score.

The rule at the time made the catch illegal if the ball had touched only Fuqua and not Tatum, since two offensive players could not combine on a deflected pass. Officials ruled it clean after conferring off the field, and film has never settled the argument. The Steelers won 13-7, their first playoff victory in 40 years as a franchise.

India were not favoured to reach the final, let alone win it. Bowled out for 183, they defended the total against a West Indies side chasing a third straight title, taking the last wicket with the total still short of India's own score. Kapil Dev's side had won only one previous World Cup match across two earlier tournaments.

The final at Lord's on 25 June 1983 was watched live back home by a much smaller television audience than later finals would draw, since few Indian households owned a set. The win is now credited with pulling investment and youth interest toward cricket in India over the following decade, reshaping the sport's centre of gravity.

Italy had been knocking on the door for years, building a case on the back of wins over the home unions in warm-up fixtures. When the invitation finally came for 2000, it turned the century-old Five Nations into six and gave a non-Celtic, non-English-speaking country a permanent seat at Europe's oldest rugby table.

Diego Dominguez kicked Italy to a 34-20 win over Scotland in Rome on 5 February 2000, their first match in the expanded championship. It remained their only Six Nations win for years afterwards, but the debut result briefly made the newcomers look like they belonged before the gap in depth reasserted itself.

Tommy Burns had ducked Jack Johnson for years, chasing bigger paydays against white contenders instead, until a promised purse of 30,000 dollars brought him to Sydney on Boxing Day 1908. Johnson outboxed him for round after round, taunting him between punches rather than ending it quickly.

By the fourteenth round Burns was staggering and unable to defend himself, and police stepped into the ring to stop the fight before a knockout could be filmed, reportedly to spare the humiliation of showing a beaten white champion on screen. Johnson was declared winner on points, the first Black heavyweight champion.

Friedrich Ludwig Jahn opened his outdoor gymnasium in the Hasenheide woods on the edge of Berlin two years after Prussia's defeat by Napoleon, and the timing was the point. Jahn believed a physically disciplined youth movement would rebuild a nation that had just lost its army, so the apparatus he designed, including early versions of the vaulting horse and balance beam, trained bodies for a future war of liberation.

The Prussian state agreed enough to ban Turnen outright in 1819, suspicious of the nationalist politics Jahn's gymnasts carried alongside their exercises, and the sites stayed closed for over a decade. Once revived, the movement spread through German-speaking Europe and into American schools, where Jahn's apparatus is still called by German names such as the pommel horse.

Figg's amphitheatre stood on Oxford Road in Marylebone, next to a tavern, not in the West End theatre district often assumed. It seated over a thousand people to watch a mixed bill: bare-knuckle boxing, but also fencing and cudgel fighting, since Figg made his living teaching all three rather than fighting full time.

He was never crowned champion in any formal sense; the title was applied to him after his death by writers looking back at an unbeaten record over roughly 270 bouts. His pupil, the boxer and painter's-model figure Jack Broughton, later drew up the sport's first written rules, carrying Figg's amphitheatre tradition into boxing's next stage.

Baseball had been played in Japan since the 1870s and toured by American all-star teams through the 1930s, including a 1934 visit built around Babe Ruth, but every domestic side before 1936 was amateur, tied to a school or a company rather than paid to play.

Seven teams launched the Japanese Baseball League that year, the country's first fully professional competition. It survived the Second World War in reduced form and was reorganised afterward into what is now Nippon Professional Baseball, still split into the Central and Pacific Leagues it adopted in 1950.

Jigoro Kano was a slight, often bullied young man who had studied several schools of jujutsu before deciding their techniques needed reworking around safety and principle rather than raw combat. In 1882 he rented rooms at the Eishoji Temple in Tokyo and opened the Kodokan with just nine students.

Kano stripped out moves he judged too dangerous for training and organised the rest around throws, pins and controlled falls that let students practise at full effort without serious injury. The school grew into judo, which he later helped bring into schools and, decades after his death, into the Olympic programme.

Bryon Russell had position, hands up, feet set. Jordan drove right, pulled up, and Russell had already lost his footing trying to recover from the initial fake. The shot fell with 5.2 seconds left in Game 6, and Utah never got a clean look back down the other end.

It was Jordan's sixth title in eight seasons with the Bulls, and the last game he played for Chicago. He walked away with a second three-peat complete, a finals MVP to match, and no farewell tour. Coach Phil Jackson and general manager Jerry Krause had already signalled the roster would be broken up regardless of the result.

Japan hosted judo's Olympic debut at the 1964 Tokyo Games expecting to sweep every weight class in the sport it had invented, and it very nearly did, winning three of the four golds on offer that year in front of enthusiastic home crowds at the Nippon Budokan, built specifically for the event.

The open weight final was the exception. Dutchman Anton Geesink, considerably larger than his Japanese opponent Akio Kaminaga, pinned him for the gold medal in front of a home crowd that fell silent. Geesink's win is still remembered in Japan as the moment judo stopped being purely a national possession and became a genuinely international sport.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar passed Wilt Chamberlain's career total of 31,419 points on 5 April 1984, in Las Vegas against the Utah Jazz, with the skyhook he had used since his UCLA days. He was 37 at the time, older than most players who hold scoring records, and had already won five NBA championships.

Chamberlain's mark had stood for a decade and looked close to permanent given how few players lasted long enough at a high scoring rate to threaten it. Abdul-Jabbar kept playing another five seasons after passing it, stretching his own total past 38,000 points before he retired in 1989.

Six teams took the field for the KBO's first pitch in 1982, each one sponsored by and named after a conglomerate rather than a city identity of its own, from the Samsung Lions to the Lotte Giants. The government under Chun Doo-hwan backed professional baseball partly to give citizens something to watch besides politics after a military takeover two years earlier.

Baseball had been played in Korea since the early twentieth century under Japanese rule, but never as a paid, organised league until this launch. The MBC Chungyong Blue Dragons and other original clubs are gone or renamed, yet the league they started grew into the country's most watched domestic sport.

Japan's oldest chronicle, the Nihon Shoki, places a kemari game in 644 as the setting for a chance meeting that would remake the country. Prince Naka no Oe, the future Emperor Tenji, lost his shoe while kicking the ball during the game, and Nakatomi no Kamatari retrieved it for him, an encounter the chronicle credits as the start of an alliance between the two men.

That alliance led directly to the Isshi Incident of 645, in which the pair killed the powerful Soga clan leader Soga no Iruka and launched the Taika Reforms that reorganised Japan's government around the emperor. Kemari itself, a non-competitive game of keeping a deerskin ball aloft using only the feet, went on to become a refined pastime of the imperial court, still practised ceremonially in Japan today.

On 6 January 1994, a man named Shane Stant struck US figure skater Nancy Kerrigan on the knee with a retractable baton as she left a practice rink in Detroit, days before the national championships that would decide the Olympic team. Kerrigan withdrew but recovered enough to compete at the Lillehammer Games weeks later.

Investigators traced the attack to Jeff Gillooly, ex-husband of rival skater Tonya Harding, and Harding's bodyguard Shawn Eckardt. Harding pleaded guilty to conspiring to hinder the prosecution afterward, was stripped of her national title and banned by US Figure Skating, while Kerrigan won Olympic silver behind Ukraine's Oksana Baiul in Lillehammer.

Jean-Claude Killy's third gold at Grenoble, in the slalom, came only after his closest rival was thrown out. Austria's Karl Schranz stopped partway down his second run, claiming a course official in dark clothing had crossed in front of him; given a rerun, he posted a faster time than Killy's. A jury later found that Schranz had already missed two gates before that interruption and disqualified him, leaving Killy the winner.

The ruling was disputed for years, with some of Schranz's supporters suggesting the mystery figure on the course had deliberately blocked him. Killy's other two golds, in downhill and giant slalom, carried no such controversy, and his sweep of every Alpine skiing event at a single Games has been matched only once since, by Austria's Toni Sailer in 1956.

Kincsem, foaled in Hungary in 1874, travelled to racecourses in England, France, Germany and Austria as well as at home, a punishing schedule for a horse of her era. She won the Goodwood Cup in England and the Grosser Preis von Baden in Germany three times, beating colts as often as fillies along the way.

By her retirement in 1879 she had started 54 times and won every one of them, a record that stayed unmatched in thoroughbred flat racing for over a century. Only Australia's Black Caviar, unbeaten in 25 starts, has come close in the years since.

Eliud Kipchoge ran 26.2 miles in 1 hour 59 minutes and 40 seconds around Vienna's Prater park in October 2019, the first time anyone had covered the marathon distance in under two hours. The run was called Ineos 1:59, staged specifically for the attempt rather than a race, with a pace car projecting laser lines and rotating teams of pacers shielding him from the wind.

Because it was not run under normal competition conditions, World Athletics never recognised it as an official world record; Kipchoge's own record, set in Berlin, stood separately. He had come close before, running 2:00:25 in a similar Nike-organised attempt in Italy in 2017, missing the two-hour mark by 25 seconds that time.

The founding story told at Edirne is a soldiers' legend rather than a record: two brothers among a company of Ottoman troops wrestled so evenly that neither could win, and both reportedly died still locked together beneath a fig tree at a spring called Kirkpinar. The tournament held there since has run most years for close to seven centuries, making it one of the oldest continuous sporting competitions anywhere.

Wrestlers coat themselves in olive oil and fight bare-chested in leather trousers called kispet, trying to lift or pin an opponent whose skin offers almost no grip. Kirkpinar is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage, and the champion still receives a golden belt rather than any modern prize money.

The Lakers were down by fourteen points at halftime against Toronto on 22 January 2006, and Kobe Bryant had scored 26 of them. He scored 55 more after the break, including 27 in the third quarter alone, on a night his teammates mostly cleared out and let him work one on one against a defence that had no answer.

His 81 points sit second only to Wilt Chamberlain's 100 in a single NBA game, a mark from 1962 that predates shot clocks being tracked the way they are today. Bryant made 28 of 46 shots and all 18 of his free throws, and the Lakers won 122-104 despite trailing for most of the first half.

Olga Korbut was 17 and stood barely five feet tall when she became the breakout star of the 1972 Munich Games, not primarily through the all-around, where a mistake on the bars cost her the title, but through sheer daring. On the uneven bars she stood on the high bar, flipped backward, and regrasped it, a release move no gymnast had shown in international competition.

Television cameras loved her: she wept openly after her error and returned days later to win gold on beam and floor. The move became known as the Korbut Flip and was later banned from the uneven bars on safety grounds, though a version survives on beam. Her performances are credited with driving a surge in gymnastics participation across the West.

Jim Laker did not simply take a lot of wickets at Old Trafford in July 1956, he took nineteen of the twenty available, finishing with figures of 9 for 37 in Australia's first innings and 10 for 53 in the second. Only Tony Lock, bowling from the other end, denied him all twenty.

The pitch, dry and crumbling under a hot week, turned sharply for both sides' spinners, and pressmen nicknamed it the beach. No bowler before or since has managed nineteen wickets in a single Test. Laker took 46 wickets across the whole series, still an England record against Australia.

Garfield Sobers had held the highest individual score in Test cricket since 1958, an innings of 365 not out that had outlasted entire generations of batsmen trying to beat it. Brian Lara arrived in Antigua in April 1994 already the world's leading run scorer that season, batting for West Indies against England in the fifth Test.

Lara batted for over twelve hours across parts of three days and finished on 375 not out, edging past Sobers by ten runs and setting a record that stood for a decade before Lara himself broke it again in 2004 with 400 not out, against the same opponent, on the same ground. The 1994 innings alone took West Indies to a total near 600.

Don Larsen had been a mediocre pitcher for most of 1956, and in his previous World Series start he had not survived the second innings. On October 8, facing the Brooklyn Dodgers in Game 5, he retired all 27 batters he faced, using only 97 pitches, needing no diving catches and no lucky bounces along the way.

The Yankees won 2-0 on solo home runs from Mickey Mantle and Hank Bauer. Larsen struck out Dale Mitchell on a called third strike to end it, and catcher Yogi Berra leapt into his arms. No pitcher has thrown a perfect game in a World Series since, and only twenty-four have ever been thrown in Major League history.

Larisa Latynina competed at three Olympics for the Soviet Union, in 1956, 1960 and 1964, and never left any of them without at least one gold medal. She was pregnant during part of her training for the 1958 world championships and returned to competition within months of giving birth.

By the end of the Tokyo Games in 1964 she had accumulated eighteen Olympic medals, nine of them gold, a total no athlete in any sport matched for 48 years. Swimmer Michael Phelps finally passed it in 2012. Latynina went on to coach the Soviet gymnastics programme for more than a decade after retiring.

Rod Laver had already completed one calendar Grand Slam in 1962, but that one came as an amateur, with the professional ranks, and the era's best players, shut out of the majors entirely. By 1969, tennis had gone open, so his second sweep, of the Australian, French, Wimbledon and US titles in a single year, meant beating every rival the sport actually had rather than a field thinned by a ban.

No man has matched it since. Laver won the US Open final in New York in September to complete the set, playing left-handed with a game built on topspin that had already made him the dominant professional of the mid-1960s. Women's tennis had its own calendar Grand Slam winner that decade too, Margaret Court, in 1970.

Cricket had been played for at least a century before anyone wrote its rules down. The London Cricket Club's code of 1744 exists mainly because heavy gambling on matches needed a fixed standard to settle disputes over: bowlers, batsmen and umpires had to agree in advance what counted as out, and how wide a pitch was fair.

The code set the pitch at 22 yards between the wickets, a length still used in every level of the game, and gave umpires final say over disputes, including the earliest reference to leg before wicket. It survives only through later copies and revisions by the Marylebone Cricket Club, which took over as the law-making body from the 1780s onward.

The crash was not caused by Pierre Levegh alone. Mike Hawthorn's Jaguar cut sharply across the track to pit, forcing Lance Macklin's Austin-Healey to swerve, and Levegh's Mercedes struck Macklin's car from behind at high speed and launched into the earthen bank fronting the grandstand.

Levegh's car disintegrated on impact. The bonnet and engine were flung into the packed crowd, and burning magnesium bodywork made the wreckage almost impossible for rescuers to approach. Levegh and roughly 83 spectators were killed. Mercedes withdrew from motor racing entirely for decades, and Switzerland banned circuit racing outright, a ban that lasted until 2015.

LeBron James passed Kareem Abdul-Jabbar for the NBA's career scoring lead on 7 February 2023, hitting a fadeaway jumper from the left elbow against the Oklahoma City Thunder for his 38,388th career point. Abdul-Jabbar's mark had stood for nearly 39 years, and Abdul-Jabbar himself was in the arena to hand James the ball afterwards.

James reached the record in 1,410 games, roughly 150 fewer than it took Abdul-Jabbar, having entered the league straight from high school in 2003 and stayed remarkably durable across two decades. The record fell during a Lakers loss, a reminder that James built the total almost entirely on nightly accumulation rather than any single scoring explosion.

Ledecky broke her own 1500m freestyle world record twice within days at the 2015 World Championships in Kazan, first in a preliminary heat, swum essentially alone against the clock rather than real competition, then again in the final. She finished the final in 15:25.48, more than half a length of the pool ahead of the field by the closing metres.

The event is rarely swum by top sprinters and rarely televised in full, which left Ledecky setting records with little of the attention a shorter race draws. She had already won 800m and 1500m golds at the 2013 Worlds as a teenager, and Kazan confirmed a stretch in which she was breaking her own distance-freestyle records almost every time she raced them seriously.

Going into the final stage of the 1989 Tour de France, Laurent Fignon led Greg LeMond by fifty seconds. That should have been safe: the stage was a 24.5 kilometre individual time trial into Paris, not the sort of terrain where such a gap usually closes. LeMond rode it on aerodynamic bars and a teardrop helmet that most of the field had not adopted.

LeMond covered the course at an average speed above 54 kilometres an hour and beat Fignon's time by fifty eight seconds, winning the Tour by eight. It remains the closest overall margin in the race's history. Fignon, riding without a helmet and reportedly in pain from saddle sores, later said he barely felt he had lost until he crossed the line.

Greg LeMond and Bernard Hinault rode for the same team in 1986, and Hinault had promised the year before to help LeMond win in return for LeMond's help in his own fifth Tour victory. Hinault instead attacked his own teammate repeatedly through the mountains, and the two argued openly about whether the deal still held.

LeMond held on to win by just over three minutes, becoming the first rider from outside Europe to win the Tour de France since it began in 1903. He had been shot in a hunting accident the previous year and needed surgery to remove pellets still lodged near his heart before he could race again.

Leonidas of Rhodes did not win one race four times, he won three separate races at the same Olympics, four Olympiads running. Starting in 164 BCE, and finishing at 152 BCE at around age 36, he swept the stadion sprint, the double-length diaulos, and the hoplitodromos, a race run in armour carrying a shield, earning the nickname Triastes, the tripler.

No ancient Olympian matched twelve individual wreaths from a single competitor for well over two thousand years. Nobody in the modern Olympics matched the underlying feat of winning across that many editions until the swimmer Michael Phelps was credited with surpassing Leonidas's overall crown count in 2016, a comparison that only works loosely since the two men competed in entirely different eras and disciplines.

The British and Irish Lions had toured New Zealand repeatedly since 1888 without ever winning a Test series against the All Blacks, losing or drawing every time. Carwyn James's 1971 squad, built around a strong Welsh core including Barry John and Gareth Edwards, went in as underdogs against a team that had not lost a home series in decades.

The Lions won the series 2-1 with one match drawn, sealing it with a draw in the final Test at Eden Park that secured the overall result. It remains the only series win by a Lions team in New Zealand; their closest repeat came in 2017, when the sides drew the series rather than either side winning it outright.

Lis Hartel had contracted polio in 1944, when she was twenty-three and already one of Denmark's leading dressage riders, and the disease left her paralysed below the knees. She competed anyway, needing to be lifted onto and off her horse Jubilee both before and after every test, and equestrian events at the time had no separate category for women; she rode against men because there was no other category to enter.

At Helsinki in 1952 she finished second to Sweden's Henri Saint Cyr, a result that opened equestrian competition to female riders at future Games. Saint Cyr lifted her from Jubilee's saddle onto the podium himself, a gesture widely photographed and remembered as much as the medal itself. She won silver again at the 1956 Stockholm Games, four years later.

Greg Louganis struck the back of his head on the springboard during a preliminary dive at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, drawing blood in the pool in front of a live audience. He received stitches, returned within the hour, and went on to win gold in that event before adding a second gold in platform days later.

Louganis knew at the time that he was HIV-positive, a fact he did not disclose publicly until 1995, and the poolside medic who treated his open wound wore no gloves. He later said he feared the blood in the water more than the injury itself, though no transmission from the incident was ever reported.

Luge had raced on the natural ice runs of the Alps for decades before it reached the Winter Olympics, and its debut at Innsbruck in 1964 was marred before it began: a British-Australian luger died in a training crash on the new artificial track, prompting safety changes to the course.

A unified German team won two of the three medal events that year, taking both men's singles and men's doubles titles. The sport has been contested at every Winter Games since, and Innsbruck's track, rebuilt after the fatal accident, hosted the Olympics again in 1976.

Larry Bird's Indiana State entered the 1979 NCAA final unbeaten at 33-0, a small-college program riding almost entirely on one player. Michigan State, led by sophomore Magic Johnson, was the more complete team, and the two men had never played each other before that Monday night in Salt Lake City.

Michigan State won 75-68, holding Bird to 19 points on poor shooting by double-teaming him all game. The broadcast drew the highest television rating any college basketball game has recorded, a figure still unmatched decades later. Johnson and Bird turned professional that year and carried their rivalry into the NBA for the next decade.

The Springbok jersey had been a symbol of white South Africa under apartheid, and many in the Black majority had cheered against the national rugby team for decades as a form of protest. When South Africa hosted the 1995 Rugby World Cup, just a year after Nelson Mandela's election, the tournament became a test of whether the team could represent the whole country rather than one part of it.

Mandela walked onto the pitch before the final wearing a green Springbok jersey and captain Francois Pienaar's number six, a gesture team members later said stunned the mostly white Ellis Park crowd into chanting his name. South Africa beat New Zealand 15-12 in extra time, with Joel Stransky's drop goal deciding it, and Mandela presented the trophy to Pienaar in the same jersey.

Diego Maradona punched the ball past England's goalkeeper Peter Shilton with his left fist in the 1986 World Cup quarter-final, and the referee missed it entirely, allowing the goal to stand. Maradona later said the goal belonged partly to the hand of God, a line that gave the incident its name and outlived the match itself.

Four minutes later he scored a second goal that needed no controversy: a run from inside his own half past five England players before rounding Shilton, later voted FIFA's Goal of the Century. Argentina won the match 2-1 and went on to beat West Germany in the final, taking the tournament in Mexico.

Wimbledon had run a men's championship since 1877 but excluded women for seven more years, on the assumption that competitive tennis was unsuitable for ladies in long skirts and corsets. When the All England Club finally relented in 1884, thirteen women entered.

Maud Watson beat her older sister Lilian in the final, 6-8, 6-3, 6-3, a family contest that set an odd precedent for a tournament meant to prove women could compete seriously. Watson defended her title the following year before Lilian eventually won it herself in 1886.

Eddy Merckx was already cycling's dominant rider, but he treated the hour record, one lap after another around a track for sixty minutes with no drafting and no pacing, as a separate kind of suffering. He chose the wooden velodrome in Mexico City for its thin, high-altitude air, which cuts wind resistance at the cost of oxygen.

On 25 October 1972 he covered 49.431 kilometres, a distance beyond any rider before him. He called it the hardest effort of his career and never attempted the record again. It stood for twelve years, until Francesco Moser broke it in 1984 using rounder, more aerodynamic wheels that Merckx never had available to him.

Milo of Croton took his first Olympic wrestling title in 532 BCE and then won four more in a row, a run ancient writers treated as effectively unbeatable rather than merely impressive. Stories about his diet, reportedly enormous quantities of meat and bread, and his strength, including carrying a bull on his shoulders, circulated for centuries and grew less credible with each retelling.

His career ended not in the ring but, according to a widely repeated but unverifiable story, when his hand became wedged in a tree trunk he had tried to split by hand and wolves found him helpless. Whatever the truth of his death, Milo's five Olympiads of wrestling dominance made him the benchmark ancient authors reached for whenever they needed to describe an athlete as the greatest of his kind.

ABC took on Monday Night Football only after CBS and NBC turned the idea down, unwilling to preempt their regular Monday lineups for a football game. ABC had little prime-time schedule to protect and gambled on it instead, hiring Howard Cosell alongside Keith Jackson and former player Don Meredith to give the broadcast a personality no Sunday game had.

The Cleveland Browns hosted the New York Jets on 21 September 1970 and won 31-21 in front of a full house at Municipal Stadium. The broadcast drew a large enough audience that ABC kept the franchise for decades, and it changed how NFL games were sold to television, turning a single weekly game into an event built around its commentary as much as its football.

The Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in December 1979, five months before it was due to host the Summer Olympics in Moscow. US President Jimmy Carter demanded the Games be moved or cancelled, and when the International Olympic Committee refused, he called for an American boycott and pressured allies to follow.

More than 60 countries stayed away, including the United States, West Germany, Japan and China, though some athletes from boycotting nations competed under neutral flags. The Soviet Union and its allies retaliated four years later by boycotting the 1984 Los Angeles Games, extending a stretch of Cold War politics that kept the world's best athletes apart across two consecutive Olympics.

The plane carrying Manchester United home from a European Cup match in Belgrade stopped to refuel in Munich on 6 February 1958. Ice on the wings meant two failed takeoff attempts, and on the third the aircraft failed to gain height, ploughed through a fence and a house, and broke apart.

Twenty-three of the 44 people aboard died, including eight players from Matt Busby's young side, nicknamed the Busby Babes, along with journalists and club staff. Busby himself was badly injured and given the last rites twice. He rebuilt the club over the following decade, and United won the European Cup in 1968 with survivor Bobby Charlton in the side.

James Naismith did not set out to invent a beloved global sport. He was a physical education instructor at the Springfield YMCA International Training School asked to devise an indoor game to keep young men active through the New England winter, and he nailed two peach baskets to a balcony rail as the targets.

His thirteen rules ran in the school's journal, The Triangle, on 15 January 1892, months after the first game was played with a soccer ball in December 1891. There was no dribbling and no backboard yet, a player could not run with the ball, and a janitor had to fetch a ladder each time someone scored.

Shah Abbas rebuilt Isfahan as his new Safavid capital around a vast rectangular square, Naqsh-e Jahan, framed by a mosque, a palace and a bazaar, and had it doubled as a polo ground where the court played and the shah could watch from a balcony. European travellers who visited the city described matches held there in front of the surrounding arcades.

Two carved stone goalposts still stand at either end of the square, and they are usually cited as the oldest polo goalposts known to survive anywhere. The square itself is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its scale, built to hold a game played on horseback, still dwarfs the market stalls and gardens that now occupy much of it.

William Hulbert ran a Chicago club frustrated with the older National Association's chaos: gambling scandals, teams that skipped games when a road trip did not pay, and no real enforcement of a schedule. In February 1876 he gathered rival owners in New York and had them sign onto a stricter, business-run league instead.

Hulbert's new league expelled two clubs, New York and Philadelphia, before the 1877 season for refusing to finish a western road trip, a signal that the old anarchy was over. It has operated continuously since 1876, and today forms one half of Major League Baseball.

NBA scores had sunk low enough by the early 1950s that teams simply held the ball once ahead; one 1950 game finished 19 to 18. Syracuse Nationals owner Danny Biasone, working with general manager Leo Ferris, tested a clock by dividing the average number of shots taken in a fast, well-played game into the game's 2,880 seconds, arriving at roughly 24 seconds per possession.

The league adopted it for the 1954 to 1955 season, and scoring jumped almost immediately, with team averages climbing by around fourteen points a game within a year. Biasone's own Nationals won the title that first season under the new rule, and the 24-second clock is now credited more than any other single change with making professional basketball watchable at the pace it is played today.

The National Basketball Association did not begin as one league finding its feet, but as two rival leagues quietly admitting neither could win alone. The Basketball Association of America, three years old and based in big-city arenas, absorbed the older, more Midwestern National Basketball League on 3 August 1949, and the combined body kept the BAA's name for its new organisation, the NBA.

Seventeen teams started the first season under the merged banner, a mix of franchises that mostly folded, moved or renamed within a decade; only a handful, including the Knicks and the Celtics, trace an unbroken line back to that 1949 roster. The rules, the ball and even the shot clock were still years from settling; the merger solved ownership, not the pace of the game itself.

Rival leagues had used a three-point shot for years, first the American Basketball League in 1961 and then the ABA from 1967, while the NBA dismissed it as a gimmick. When the NBA absorbed several ABA teams in 1976, the case for adopting the line grew hard to ignore, and it was added for the 1979-80 season.

Chris Ford of the Boston Celtics made the league's first three-pointer, against the Houston Rockets on 12 October 1979, the season's opening night. The shot was treated as a minor rule change at the time; players attempted only about two per game per team that first season, a rate that has since risen more than tenfold across the league.

Andrew Rube Foster, a former pitcher turned team owner, brought together the owners of eight Midwestern clubs at a Kansas City YMCA to sign the league's founding agreement. He wrote much of its structure himself and kept close personal control over scheduling and player movement between teams for most of its existence.

Earlier Black teams had barnstormed for decades, but none had run a stable season-long schedule with a champion crowned at the end of it. The league lasted until 1931, folding soon after Foster's health broke down, and its example shaped the Negro American League and later circuits that followed it.

Nero did not simply win a rigged race in 67 CE, he lost one in public. Racing a ten-horse chariot, an entry stacked in his favour, he was thrown from the car partway through and failed to finish. Olympic judges declared him the winner anyway, since delaying his own imperial visit to Greece was not something anyone present wanted to risk.

Nero had already forced the Greek Games' organisers to move the entire festival's date to fit his tour schedule and to add musical and poetry contests he was confident of winning outright. Once he was dead the following year, Greek officials struck his chariot victory from the record books, one of the few Olympic titles ever formally erased rather than merely disputed by later historians.

Charles II raced his own horses at Newmarket and rode in some of the matches himself, which is why the Town Plate of 1665 carried royal authority rather than a local club's. He wrote out the conditions personally: a set weight for each horse, a fixed distance and an order of running, replacing the informal wagers that had governed racing before it.

The race is still run at Newmarket most years, making it one of the oldest continuously staged sporting fixtures anywhere. Its significance is less the contest itself than the precedent: a written code, issued by the state's highest authority, that other courses and clubs then copied when they organised their own meetings.

The league that became the NFL was agreed on in Ralph Hay's Hupmobile showroom in Canton, Ohio, where team owners sat on the running boards and fenders of cars because there were not enough chairs. Jim Thorpe, already a national sports celebrity, was named the American Professional Football Association's first president that same afternoon.

Thorpe's title was largely a drawing card rather than an executive role, and the league dropped its original name for the National Football League only two years later. Canton's Bulldogs, one of the founding franchises, is the reason the Pro Football Hall of Fame sits in that city rather than a larger market.

Jack Nicklaus had not won a major in six years and a newspaper columnist wrote him off as finished before the final round of the 1986 Masters even began. He shot a back nine of 30, six under par, to overtake the leaders and win his sixth green jacket at Augusta National.

At 46 he became the oldest Masters champion, a record that still stands, and his eighteenth major overall remains the most any golfer has won. His son Jackie carried his bag that week, and the roar that followed his eagle on the fifteenth hole is still cited as one of the loudest moments in golf broadcasting.

The circuit was built through the Eifel mountains partly as a public works project to bring jobs to a depressed rural region, using largely manual labour to carve roughly 28 kilometres of combined track through forest and farmland. It opened in June 1927 with a motorcycle race, followed the next day by cars.

The Nordschleife, its northern loop of around 22 kilometres with more than 150 corners and severe elevation changes, earned the nickname The Green Hell decades later from Formula One driver Jackie Stewart. It hosted grands prix and endurance races for most of the twentieth century and remains a public toll road when it is not booked for racing.

Nyad had tried the crossing four times before, starting in 1978, and each attempt had failed to jellyfish stings, storms or exhaustion. She returned at 64 with a silicone mask to blunt box jellyfish venom and a support team tracking sharks from kayaks, rather than the cage that had disqualified an earlier attempt from record consideration.
