She left Havana on 31 August 2013 and reached Key West on 2 September, roughly 53 hours later, becoming the first person to complete the swim without a shark cage. It was her fifth attempt across 35 years, and she walked up the beach still talking, telling the crowd waiting for her that people should never give up.

Before 1925 an attacker needed three opposing players, usually two defenders plus the goalkeeper, between them and the goal to stay onside. The law was rewritten so only two opponents were required, effectively halving the space defences had to police and immediately opening up forward play.

Goal totals jumped sharply the following season; some English First Division clubs scored dozens more league goals than the year before. Offside trap tactics that had flattened scoring through the early 1920s lost much of their power, and the two-opponent version of the rule, with later tweaks, is still the basis of the law today.

Pierre de Coubertin sketched the five interlocking rings in 1913, colouring them blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white background, a combination he chose because at least one of those colours appeared on every national flag in the world at the time. He first showed the design publicly in a 1913 letter and had it printed on stationery that year.

The symbol did not appear at an actual Olympics until 1920 in Antwerp, after the 1916 Berlin Games were cancelled by the First World War. Coubertin's own explanation, that the five rings represented the union of five inhabited continents rather than any specific set of nations, has stuck as the design's official meaning ever since.

Softball had been played competitively by women in the United States since the early twentieth century, but it took decades of lobbying by international federations before the International Olympic Committee added it to the programme for the 1996 Atlanta Games, using the fast-pitch variant rather than the slower recreational style.

Eight teams competed in a round-robin format, and the United States, led by pitcher Lisa Fernandez and outfielder Dot Richardson, went undefeated through the tournament to win the first gold medal, beating China in the final. The sport was dropped from the Olympic programme after 2008 before being reinstated for select later Games including Tokyo 2020.

New Zealand's 1905 touring side did not go unbeaten. Of 35 matches played across Britain, Ireland, France and North America, they won 34, and the single defeat came against Wales at Cardiff Arms Park, a 3-0 loss still argued over for a disputed try that was never allowed.

The scoreline elsewhere was lopsided: 976 points scored to 59 conceded, and 243 tries in the tour overall. Playing entirely in black jerseys with a silver fern, the team gave New Zealand rugby the nickname and the reputation that followed every side to wear it afterward.

Francis Ouimet was a 20-year-old amateur who had grown up across the street from The Country Club in Brookline, Massachusetts, caddying there before he ever played it in competition. He forced a playoff after tying England's Harry Vardon and Ted Ray at the end of regulation in the 1913 U.S. Open.

In the 18-hole playoff Ouimet shot a level 72 against Vardon's 77 and Ray's 78, staying bogey-free on the back nine while his ten-year-old caddie, Eddie Lowery, kept him calm. The win, by an unpaid amateur over golf's two biggest professional names, is widely credited with turning golf into a game Americans followed rather than one they merely read about.

Cricket's bowling arm had already crept upward for decades before 1864: underarm gave way to round-arm deliveries in the early nineteenth century, each change fought over by traditionalists who thought a raised arm was closer to throwing than bowling. The Marylebone Cricket Club settled the argument on 10 June 1864 by rewriting Law 10 to permit any height of arm, provided it stayed straight and the ball was not thrown.

The change let bowlers generate far more pace and bounce than round-arm technique allowed, reshaping how batsmen defended and how fast bowling developed for the rest of the century. By the time Test cricket began in 1877, overarm was already the default method, though some underarm bowling persisted at lower levels into the early twentieth century.

Jesse Owens arrived in Ann Arbor on 25 May 1935 for a Big Ten conference meet barely able to bend after falling down a flight of stairs days earlier, and needed a hot bath before he could compete at all. He then tied the world 100-yard record at 9.4 seconds and moved on to three individual events.

In the long jump he reached 26 feet 8 and a quarter inches, a world record that stood for 25 years; he then set world records in the 220-yard sprint and the 220-yard low hurdles. Four world records and a tie, inside 45 minutes, on a track he had never seen before that afternoon.

Paavo Nurmi ran the 1500 metres and the 5000 metres at the 1924 Paris Olympics within about an hour of each other, on the same afternoon, and won both. He trained with a stopwatch in hand, pacing himself lap by lap rather than reacting to rivals, a method almost unheard of among distance runners at the time.

He added three more golds in Paris, including the individual and team cross-country races run in punishing heat that put several other competitors in hospital. Nurmi finished the games with five gold medals from a single Olympics, a total matched by few track athletes since.

Long before Chichen Itza or any Aztec temple existed, villagers on Mexico's Pacific coast dug a shallow earthen alley about 80 metres long and lined it with clay embankments for spectators. Archaeologists dated it to roughly 1650 BCE, making it the oldest formal sporting structure yet found in the Americas, centuries before the ballgame appears in any Olmec or Maya carving.

No ball or hoop survived at Paso de la Amada itself, but rubber balls from the same region and period confirm the game it served. The court sat beside what may have been a chief's residence, hinting that hosting matches was already bound up with political status. Over the next 3,000 years the ballgame spread across Mesoamerica, eventually acquiring the stone walls and ceremonial stakes seen at later sites.

No NFL team had finished a regular season 16-0 before New England did it in 2007, a run built on Tom Brady throwing a then-record 50 touchdown passes and Randy Moss catching 23 of them. The Patriots also spent that season under investigation for illegally filming opponents' defensive signals, a scandal known as Spygate that shadowed the perfect run.

The undefeated streak reached 18-0 through the playoffs before the New York Giants beat them in Super Bowl XLII on a fourth-quarter touchdown drive capped by Plaxico Burress, a finish still replayed as one of the biggest upsets in Super Bowl history. New England's 2007 season ended one win short of the only perfect year in modern NFL play.

Phar Lap went off at odds of 8 to 11 for the 1930 Melbourne Cup, still the shortest price ever accepted on a Cup favourite. Bookmakers had been so alarmed by his form that an attempt was made to shoot him days before the race, and he ran under armed guard.

The New Zealand-bred gelding carried the extra weight of a champion's handicap and still won easily at Flemington. He died in California less than two years later, officially of colic, though the sudden death of Australia's most popular sporting figure fed suspicion of poisoning for decades.

Mark Spitz's seven gold medals from the 1972 Munich Games had been swimming's benchmark for 36 years, and Spitz himself said in the run-up to Beijing that he doubted anyone would beat it, since modern programmes spread swimmers across fewer events. Phelps entered eight in Beijing and needed every one of them to go right.

The closest was the 100m butterfly, won by one hundredth of a second over Serbia's Milorad Cavic on a stroke that photo review had to confirm touched the wall first. Phelps's medley relay team also had to hold off France on the final leg. Eight golds from eight finals in one Games remains a record no swimmer has matched since.

Around 70 BCE two local magistrates, Gaius Quinctius Valgus and Marcus Porcius, paid for an amphitheatre at Pompeii out of their own money, according to an inscription they left on its walls. It is the oldest Roman amphitheatre known to survive, built decades before Rome's own Colosseum, and it used the town's natural slope so that earth banked against the outer wall did much of the structural work.

Unlike later imperial arenas, it had no substructure of animal cages or trapdoors beneath the floor; games there relied on what could be brought in overland. Buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE, it survived intact enough that its oval shape and seating tiers remain walkable today, a rare look at how a provincial town staged its own games.

Red Grange turned professional the day after his final college game at Illinois in 1925, joining George Halas's Chicago Bears in a move college football's own establishment treated as close to scandalous, since turning pro for money was seen as beneath a star amateur. His coach at Illinois publicly disowned the decision.

Grange and the Bears then played a barnstorming tour of roughly 19 games in under two months, drawing 68,000 fans to New York's Polo Grounds alone. Gate receipts that large were unheard of for a pro football game, and the tour is generally credited with keeping the fledgling league solvent through its early, precarious years.

Red Rum had already won the Grand National twice, in 1973 and 1974, and finished second the following two years, an unheard-of run of consistency over Aintree's 30 punishing fences. Trainer Ginger McCain worked him on the beach at Southport, partly because the horse had a bone disease that the salt water seemed to ease.

In 1977, aged 12, Red Rum won a third National, a feat no horse has repeated. He led from the front and pulled away in the final stretch under jockey Tommy Stack. He never raced again, retiring as the only horse to win the race three times, and lived out his years as a fixture of Aintree ceremonies until his death in 1995.

Boston had sold Babe Ruth to the Yankees in the winter of 1919, and blamed the following eight decades of near misses on the sale ever after, most painfully a Game 6 error in 1986 that let the Mets extend a World Series Boston was one out from winning. The nickname stuck because the losing kept finding new ways to happen.

The 2004 Red Sox had been down three games to none to the Yankees in the American League Championship Series, a deficit no team in baseball history had overcome, before winning four straight to reach the World Series. They then swept St Louis in four games, and the Curse of the Bambino talk stopped almost overnight.

English referee Ken Aston devised the system after a 1966 World Cup quarter-final he officiated ended in confusion over whether a player had actually been sent off, with no clear signal understood across languages. Sitting at a traffic light some time later, he settled on the same colours: yellow to slow down, red to stop.

FIFA introduced the cards at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico, and yellow ones came out often, five players were booked in the opening match alone between the hosts and the Soviet Union. No player was actually sent off with a red card during that tournament; the first World Cup red card was not shown until 1974, once referees had grown more willing to use it.

Redgrave had said after Atlanta in 1996 that anyone who saw him near a boat again had permission to shoot him. He was rowing again within months, chasing a fifth consecutive gold despite being diagnosed with diabetes and colitis in the years between, conditions that forced him to manage insulin around a training schedule built for endurance.

In the coxless four at Sydney, his crew of Redgrave, James Cracknell, Tim Foster and Matthew Pinsent held off Italy by three tenths of a second. It made Redgrave the only man to win gold at five consecutive Olympics in an endurance sport, a record British rowing still measures itself against.

Rhythmic gymnastics had existed as a competitive sport since the 1940s in the Soviet Union, built out of dance and calisthenics traditions rather than the tumbling roots of artistic gymnastics. It took until the 1984 Los Angeles Games for the International Olympic Committee to admit it, and only in an individual all-around format.

Canada's Lori Fung won that first gold with a routine using a rope, edging out competitors from countries with far longer traditions in the discipline. Soviet-bloc gymnasts, who had shaped the sport for decades, were absent from Los Angeles entirely because the Soviet Union boycotted the Games that year.

Lou Gehrig's streak of 2,130 consecutive games, built between 1925 and 1939, had been one of baseball's supposedly unbreakable records, ended only by the illness that later took his name. Cal Ripken Jr. of the Baltimore Orioles had been quietly chasing it for years without missing a game for injury, benching or rest.

On 6 September 1995, Ripken played his 2,131st consecutive game against the California Angels at Camden Yards, and the number became official once the game passed the point of an early rain-out. He circled the stadium shaking fans' hands as a 22-minute standing ovation ran on, and he extended the streak further before voluntarily ending it in 1998 at 2,632 games.

Maurice Richard thought he had his fiftieth goal a day early, in a win over Chicago on 17 March 1945, but the goal was disallowed. He got the real one the next night, 18 March, against Boston goaltender Harvey Bennett, in Montreal's fiftieth and final game of the season, tying the score before Elmer Lach put the Canadiens ahead.

The record was a kind of dare for thirty-six years: no one else reached fifty in fifty games until Mike Bossy in 1981, and only Wayne Gretzky ever beat the pace outright, reaching fifty in thirty-nine. Richard's own total that season, fifty goals in fifty games exactly, broke a mark Joe Malone had held since the league's first season in 1917.

Rowing was meant to debut at the very first modern Olympics in 1896, and two four-oar crews actually reached the start line at the Bay of Zea. Strong winds forced a postponement, and organisers eventually abandoned the competition entirely rather than reschedule it into an already tight programme, leaving the sport out of the results.

It finally ran at Paris in 1900, staged on the Seine at Courbevoie with four events and crews from several European nations. The river's currents and narrow course caused their own problems, but the races were completed this time, and rowing has been part of the Summer Games at every edition held since.

The organisation had already existed for 27 years as the Northern Union, formed in 1895 when 22 clubs split from rugby's governing body over paying players for missed work. The 1922 change of name to the Rugby Football League was administrative rather than a rupture in the game itself, tidying up what the code was actually called.

The rebrand followed the sport's spread beyond its original Yorkshire and Lancashire heartlands and matched the label already used informally by players and the press. Rugby league has kept that name since, distinguishing it permanently from the rugby union code it split from decades earlier.

Rugby football had spread for decades with no fixed rulebook: clubs argued endlessly over whether hacking, tripping an opponent below the knee, belonged in the game. On 26 January 1871, representatives of 21 London and provincial clubs met at the Pall Mall Restaurant to settle it by founding a governing body.

The new Rugby Football Union banned hacking outright within weeks, a decision that split off soccer's ancestors years earlier but still angered traditionalists within rugby itself. The laws it drafted that year became the basis for the sport played today, and the Union still governs English rugby.

The vote that split rugby league from rugby union for good was not close: Warrington moved that the Northern Union play thirteen a side instead of fifteen, and delegates passed it 43 votes to 18 in 1906. A Warrington official argued the smaller side would also save struggling clubs around 100 pounds a year in wages.

The same reform replaced the contested ruck with the play-the-ball, where a tackled player restarts play by heeling the ball back rather than fighting for it in a scrum-like pile. Together the changes opened up the game, and the 1906-07 season that followed saw a marked jump in tries scored.

Rugby union had enforced strict amateurism since the sport's 1895 split from rugby league, a schism triggered when northern English clubs wanted to pay players for missed work and the union authorities refused. For a century, union players could not be paid even as the game filled stadiums and drew television deals, while top players increasingly switched codes or threatened to for money.

Facing pressure from a breakaway professional circuit being organised in the southern hemisphere, the International Rugby Board declared the sport open in August 1995, letting players and unions accept payment for the first time. Clubs and national bodies scrambled to restructure finances within months, and player wages, transfer-style movement and full-time training regimes followed within a few seasons.

George Foreman had knocked out Joe Frazier and Ken Norton, both men who had beaten Muhammad Ali, and entered the fight in Kinshasa on 30 October 1974 unbeaten and a heavy favourite. Ali, at 32, was not expected to survive Foreman's power for long, and few observers gave him a real chance.

Ali spent round after round leaning back against the ropes, letting Foreman punch himself tired, a tactic he called rope-a-dope. In the eighth round Ali came off the ropes and knocked Foreman down; he did not get up. An estimated one billion people watched worldwide, then the largest television audience for any event.

Sadaharu Oh played his entire career in Japan for the Yomiuri Giants, so his pursuit of the home run record drew far less attention in the United States than Hank Aaron's had. He had already passed Babe Ruth's 714 in 1976, and by September 1977 he was closing on Aaron's total of 755.

On 3 September 1977, before 55,000 fans at Korakuen Stadium in Tokyo, he cleared the fence off Yakult pitcher Kojiro Suzuki to pass Aaron and become the world's all-time leader. He retired in 1980 with 868, a total no major league player has approached, though the shorter Japanese season and different competition level keep the comparison contested among historians of the game.

The Football Act passed by James I's parliament grouped football with golf as games to be stopped, ordering that no man play at 'fut ball' and setting a fine of fourpence for anyone caught. The concern, as in England, was that football and golf were pulling men away from archery practice needed for national defence.

The fine was real money for a labourer, yet the law was reissued by later Scottish parliaments in 1457, 1471 and 1491, each time complaining that the previous ban had been ignored. Golf survived those repeated attempts to suppress it and eventually outgrew archery in Scottish life, while football kept being played in towns regardless of the fine.

Sumo existed in Japan long before Emperor Shomu's reign, but in 726 he turned it into a fixed feature of court life, staging wrestling matches as part of an annual palace ritual known as sechie-zumo. Wrestlers were summoned from the provinces to compete before the throne, and the outcomes were sometimes read as omens for the coming harvest, tying the sport to agricultural anxiety rather than pure entertainment.

The tournament format under later emperors added referees, ranked wrestlers, and elaborate ceremony, laying groundwork for conventions still visible in professional sumo, including ring-entering rituals performed before a bout. Court sumo declined as imperial authority weakened, but the sport survived by moving from palace ritual into wider popular entertainment.

Secretariat won the Kentucky Derby and the Preakness by two and a half lengths each, close enough that his Triple Crown was still in doubt going into the Belmont Stakes on 9 June 1973. He was America's first Triple Crown winner in 25 years, since Citation in 1948, and the pressure on the horse and his jockey, Ron Turcotte, was considerable.

He won the Belmont by 31 lengths, a margin of about 253 feet, in a time of 2:24 that remains the fastest the race has ever been run. Turcotte later said he had no idea how far ahead he was until he glanced back near the finish. No horse has since come within 20 lengths of matching that margin.

Short track speed skating had existed as an informal pack sport for decades before the International Olympic Committee added it as a medal discipline at the 1992 Albertville Games, having tested it as a demonstration event four years earlier in Calgary. Four events were contested: men's and women's 500m and 1000m, plus the relays that would be added the same Games.

Skaters raced in packs of four to six on a tight 111 metre oval rather than the two-at-a-time pursuit format of long track, making contact, blocked passes and disqualifications part of the sport from its first Olympic outing. South Korea, which had built a domestic programme around the discipline through the 1980s, won two of the four available golds.

Bobby Thomson's home run did not win a routine game; it won a pennant the Giants had trailed the Dodgers by thirteen and a half games for in August, before an extraordinary late-season collapse forced a three-game playoff. On 3 October 1951 at the Polo Grounds, with the Giants down by two runs in the ninth inning, Thomson pulled a fastball from Ralph Branca into the left-field stands.

Radio announcer Russ Hodges's call, repeating the Giants win the pennant four times, became as famous as the swing itself. Decades later, several Giants players admitted the team had been stealing opposing catchers' signs from a telescope in the clubhouse that season, a claim that has never been proven to apply to that specific pitch but complicates the moment's legend regardless.

The 1985 World Snooker Championship final ran past midnight, and by the time Dennis Taylor potted the last black to beat Steve Davis 18-17, an audience of 18.5 million was still watching on BBC Two. It remains the largest late-night television audience recorded in Britain, a figure helped by nobody expecting the match to run that long.

Taylor had trailed 8-0 early in the final and looked finished before rallying through the closing session. He wore upside-down spectacles fitted with prisms to see the table clearly under the overhead lights, an eccentric detail that made him instantly recognisable and turned an underdog's comeback into the sport's signature night.

Neville Chamberlain, a British army officer stationed at Jubbulpore, added coloured balls to the existing game of black pool in the officers' mess in 1875. When a player fluffed a shot, fellow officers jeered him as a snooker, army slang for a first-year cadet, and the name stuck to the whole game.

Chamberlain only wrote down his claim to have invented it in a 1938 letter to a sporting magazine, more than sixty years after the fact, by which point the game had already spread through British clubs and colonial messes worldwide. Governing bodies now accept his account as the origin of the sport.

The first Olympic snowboard gold, in the men's giant slalom at Nagano, went to Canada's Ross Rebagliati. Two days later the IOC stripped it after he tested positive for marijuana, then restored it when Canada argued the drug was not on the banned list for that event. He kept the medal.

The sport had spent years lobbying to be taken seriously by a federation built around skiing, and many competitors distrusted the fit even as they arrived. Halfpipe and giant slalom were the two disciplines contested that year, both won by North Americans, before snowboarding expanded steadily at every Games after.

Twenty-two noblemen and gentlemen founded the society in 1754 mainly to compete for a silver club, copying the format Edinburgh's golfers had set up ten years earlier at Leith. St Andrews had no special status yet; it was one golfing town among several with an organised club and a set of borrowed rules.

The society took the name Royal and Ancient in 1834 after William IV agreed to be its patron, and it grew into the body that still writes and interprets golf's rules jointly with the United States Golf Association. The Old Course at St Andrews became golf's reference point largely because this club, and not any inherent claim to the game's origin, was based there.

The story starts with a football score, not a baseball. Alumni of the Farragut Boat Club in Chicago gathered on Thanksgiving Day 1887 to hear the Yale-Harvard result by telegraph, and a Yale supporter hurled a boxing glove at a Harvard fan in celebration.

George Hancock, a reporter watching the scene, tied the glove into a rough ball and called out to play, chalking a diamond onto the clubhouse floor and using a broom handle for a bat. The indoor game he improvised that afternoon became softball, and Hancock is credited as its inventor.

Six of the seven judges put Sonja Henie first in a field of twenty skaters at the 1928 St Moritz Games, and at fifteen she became the youngest individual gold medallist in Winter Olympic history, a record that stood for 74 years. Norwegian judges were not among those swayed; the vote crossed borders.

Henie had trained as a dancer before she skated, and she brought short skirts, jumps borrowed from ballet, and choreographed programmes into a sport that had rewarded stiff, formal figures. She went on to win gold again in 1932 and 1936, then moved to Hollywood, where her films made her one of the highest-paid stars of the era.

The Old Bowling Green sits beside Southampton's medieval town walls, and the club that maintains it traces continuous play back to 1299, a claim resting on local record rather than a single dated document. What makes it notable is not the origin story but the unbroken use: bowls has been played on the same patch of turf for over seven centuries.

Green bowls of this period had none of the modern game's biased woods, and matches were as likely to be about wagering as sport. Southampton's green survived enclosure, siege and two world wars intact, and the club still plays there today, which is the whole basis of the record.

Mark Spitz had already been humiliated once at an Olympics: in Mexico City in 1968 he predicted six golds and won two. In Munich in 1972 he swam seven events and won all seven, each in a new world record, a feat no swimmer had matched before or has matched since in a single Games.

The mark stood for 36 years, until Michael Phelps won eight golds in Beijing in 2008. Spitz's moustache became as famous as the medals; he swam with it rather than shaving it, joking it helped divert water from his mouth. He retired from competitive swimming within a year of Munich, aged 22.

The earliest known mention of stoolball is not a sports report but a complaint: a manual written to instruct parish priests scolds clergy for playing 'at the ball' in churchyards, including a game called stoolball, calling it unbecoming of their office. That the game needed condemning at all suggests it was already common enough to be a nuisance.

Stoolball had a batter defending a stool or post against a thrown ball, and some historians treat it as an ancestor of both cricket and rounders, though the line of descent is guesswork rather than record. It survived longest in Sussex and Kent, where women's leagues still play a version of it today.

Naim Suleymanoglu weighed barely 60 kilograms yet clean and jerked 190 kilograms at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, more than three times his own bodyweight, setting a world record in the process. Turkish officials had paid Bulgaria a reported sum to let him leave and compete for Turkey after he defected the year before.

He set three world records across the snatch, clean and jerk, and total in the featherweight division at a single Games, a sweep that earned him the nickname Pocket Hercules. Suleymanoglu went on to win gold at two more Olympics, but Seoul was the meet where a defector barely out of his teens rewrote his weight class.

The figure is barely palm-sized: two men gripping identical belts around each other's waists, cast in copper around 2600 BCE and buried in the Nintu temple at Khafajah, in modern Iraq. Nobody recorded their names or the occasion. The belt grip itself survived far longer than the bronze, turning up centuries later in Mongolian and Turkish wrestling styles that still lock hands on a rival's sash.

Khafajah was a minor city in the Diyala River valley, excavated in the 1930s alongside temples to several Sumerian deities. The wrestlers were found among votive offerings rather than trophies, suggesting the object marked devotion rather than a particular match. It is one of the earliest pieces of evidence that organised, rule-bound combat sport existed before writing had fully settled into narrative record.

Canada had never faced the Soviet national team before 1972, and the eight-game Summit Series was billed as a formality for the country that invented the sport. The Soviets won the opener 7-3 in Montreal. Canada trailed the series going into the final game in Moscow, needing a win to avoid an outcome many at home found unthinkable.

Paul Henderson scored the winner with 34 seconds left in Game 8, his second goal of the period, giving Canada a 6-5 victory and the series. Broadcaster Foster Hewitt's call of the goal is still replayed across Canada each September. Henderson never scored another goal of comparable consequence in his NHL career.

Baltimore had won 13 of 14 regular-season games and entered as roughly 18-point favourites, a gap so wide that some bookmakers stopped offering the bet. Joe Namath told a banquet crowd three nights before the game that the Jets would win, a guarantee sportswriters treated as bravado from the AFL's least credible franchise.

Namath did not throw a touchdown pass in the game, handing off often and letting Matt Snell run for a score, but he was named the game's most valuable player anyway for managing the Jets to a 16-7 win. The result forced the NFL establishment to take the rival AFL seriously a year before the two leagues fully merged, and Kansas City's win the following January confirmed it was not a fluke.

Atlanta led 28 to 3 early in the third quarter of Super Bowl LI in February 2017, and the Falcons' win probability models had them near certain winners. New England scored 25 unanswered points, forcing overtime for the first time in the game's history, before James White's short touchdown run won it 34 to 28.

Tom Brady threw for 466 yards, a Super Bowl record, and finished the comeback with a two-point conversion pass to Danny Amendola that tied the score at 28 with under a minute left in regulation. Atlanta's offence never touched the ball in overtime under the sudden-death rules then in place.

Synchronised swimming reached the Olympics in 1984 only in solo and duet form, an odd choice for a sport built around groups moving in unison, because team events were not added until 1996. Judges scored routines on figures performed without music as well as a final set piece performed to it.

The sport had grown out of water ballet exhibitions popular in the early twentieth century and had been trying to reach Olympic status since the 1950s. Canada's Carolyn Waldo and the American duet of Candy Costie and Tracie Ruiz won the first golds at the Los Angeles Games, held in the same pool complex as diving.

Table tennis had been a mass participation sport across Asia and Europe for decades before the International Olympic Committee finally added it at the 1988 Seoul Games, in singles and doubles for both men and women. China, which had dominated world championships since the 1960s, entered as the clear favourite.

China and South Korea split the first gold medals between them, with China winning both women's events and South Korea's Yoo Nam-kyu taking men's singles on home tables. The sport's late arrival meant several established world champions were already past their prime by the time an Olympic medal became available to them.

Taekwondo had already appeared as a demonstration sport at two earlier Olympics, in 1988 and 1992, before the IOC finally granted it full medal status for Sydney in 2000. The wait mattered to South Korea, where the sport had been made compulsory in schools and promoted as a piece of national identity abroad.

Eight weight categories were contested, four for men and four for women, each nation limited to one entrant per division to spread the medals around. Cuba and South Korea dominated the inaugural tally, and the sport's Olympic status gave it a training and funding pipeline that folk martial arts rarely get.

Korea had no single martial art called taekwondo before 1955. What existed was a scattering of kwans, private schools teaching variants of Japanese karate adapted after liberation from colonial rule in 1945, each with its own name and lineage and little agreement on technique.

General Choi Hong Hi chaired a naming committee that settled on taekwondo, meaning foot hand way, to unify those schools under one Korean identity rather than a borrowed Japanese one. Choi later founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation, though the sport eventually split into rival federations that still coexist today.

Amateur tennis had been a polite fiction for years before 1968: leading players took under-the-table payments while officially unpaid, and the top professionals, banned from the Grand Slams, played a separate barnstorming circuit for cash. The British Lawn Tennis Association forced the issue that spring by declaring Wimbledon open to professionals regardless of what the international federation decided.

The first open Grand Slam, the French Championships in Paris that May, let amateurs and professionals compete on the same draw for the first time. Rod Laver won the men's title there and at Wimbledon weeks later. The change also opened the door to prize money for women, though pay disparity between the men's and women's game persisted for years afterward.

Olympia added its first event that did not require a human body to do the running in 680 BCE: the tethrippon, four horses yoked to a light two-wheeled chariot, racing roughly twelve laps of the hippodrome. The prize went to the owner, not the driver, which meant wealthy patrons who never touched the reins could still be crowned Olympic victors, and several were women barred from competing in person.

The course was dangerous by design, with a tight turning post at each end that regularly overturned chariots at speed. Crashes were common enough that ancient accounts treat a clean finish as noteworthy in itself. The event pulled Olympia's prestige toward wealth and ownership rather than pure athletic feat, a tension that later let non-competitors like Roman emperors claim victories they never physically earned.

England had never lost a Test on home soil until Australia beat them at The Oval in August 1882 by seven runs, chasing a target of 85 that England somehow failed to reach. The defeat was small in scale and enormous in effect: it was the first time Australia had won in England at all.

Days later the Sporting Times printed a mock obituary announcing that English cricket had died and its body would be cremated, its ashes taken to Australia. When England toured there that winter, a group of Melbourne women presented captain Ivo Bligh with a small urn, and the joke became the name of the fixture.

Brazil did not need to win the final to take the 1950 World Cup, only draw it, since the tournament's closing group put the title on goal difference rather than a knockout. Newspapers had already printed victory editions and a samba had been written for the occasion. Uruguay went behind, then scored twice through Juan Alberto Schiaffino and Alcides Ghiggia, winning 2 to 1 in front of a crowd inside the Maracana usually put near 200,000.

Ghiggia later said only three people had ever silenced the Maracana: Frank Sinatra, Pope John Paul II, and himself. Brazil's shock defeat left such a mark on the national game that the team abandoned its all-white kit afterward, switching to the yellow shirt now inseparable from Brazilian football.

Theagenes of Thasos claimed the Olympic boxing title in 480 BCE, then returned four years later to add the pankration as well, a brutal combination event mixing striking and grappling. Only one other ancient athlete, Kleitomachos of Thebes, is recorded winning both disciplines at Olympia, and he did it in a single Games rather than across two.

Ancient sources credit Theagenes with more than 1,400 victories across the Panhellenic circuit, including the Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean games, a figure impossible to verify but repeated by writers close enough to his lifetime to have known his reputation firsthand. After his death the people of Thasos worshipped him as a healing god, and the sick reportedly slept beside his statue hoping for a cure.

Land speed record attempts had crept toward the speed of sound for years without crossing it, since the shockwaves a vehicle generates near Mach 1 can destabilise it at ground level in ways aircraft rarely encounter at altitude. ThrustSSC was built around two Rolls Royce Spey turbofan jet engines, the same type used in some fighter jets, mounted either side of a slender twin hull.

On 15 October 1997, RAF pilot Andy Green drove ThrustSSC across Nevada's Black Rock Desert at a two-way average of 763.035 mph, equivalent to Mach 1.02, officially breaking the sound barrier on land for the first time. The record has not been beaten since, and a planned successor project, Bloodhound, has yet to attempt a run at that speed.

Tiger Woods had not won a major since 2008, and by 2017 a fused spine had left him barely able to swing a club. Two years later, at the 2019 Masters, he closed with a one-under 70 and held off Francesco Molinari and Brooks Koepka on the back nine at Augusta National to win by a single stroke, his 15th major title.

The gallery around the 18th green that Sunday was so dense that patrons and past champions abandoned their own rounds to watch him finish. It was Woods's first Masters win without holding at least a share of the lead after 54 holes, and it came eleven years after his previous major, at the 2008 US Open.

Old Tom Morris had held the record margin in a major since 1862, thirteen strokes at the Open Championship. Woods beat it by two at Pebble Beach in June 2000, finishing at twelve under while nobody else in the field broke par for the tournament, on a course the USGA had set up to punish any loose shot.

He closed at 272, fifteen strokes clear of the tied runners-up, Ernie Els and Miguel Angel Jimenez. It was the third leg of what golf writers started calling the Tiger Slam once he added the Open Championship and PGA Championship that summer and the Masters the following April, four consecutive majors held by one player.

Tom Simpson collapsed a mile from the summit of Mont Ventoux on 13 July 1967 and died shortly after, during the thirteenth stage of the Tour de France. A post-mortem found amphetamines and alcohol in his body, a combination that, mixed with heat and dehydration on the exposed final climb, proved fatal. He had continued riding, and been helped back onto his bike, in the minutes before he fell for the last time.

The line most attached to his death, put me back on my bike, is widely repeated but poorly sourced; his mechanic Harry Hall, who was beside him, recalled Simpson saying only on, on, on. Simpson remains British cycling's most cited case for why the sport tightened anti-doping controls, though systematic testing did not follow for years.

Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean spent most of their four minutes on the ice at the 1984 Sarajevo Olympics kneeling or crouched, a deliberate reading of the rules that a routine need not be skated upright throughout. Their programme to Ravel's Bolero earned nine perfect 6.0 scores for artistic impression, a result no ice dance pair has matched since.

Olympic rules capped a free dance at four minutes ten seconds, but no arranger could trim Bolero below four minutes twenty eight. Torvill and Dean noticed the clock only started once a blade touched the ice, so they opened kneeling and motionless, buying eighteen seconds before Torvill first skated, and finished with time to spare.

George Nissen was a competitive tumbler at the University of Iowa who had watched circus trapeze artists drop into safety nets and wondered whether a taut bounce could be built for its own sake. With his coach Larry Griswold, he stretched canvas across a steel frame using rubber inner-tube strips instead of springs.

Nissen named it the trampoline after the Spanish word for diving board, trampolin, and later took the apparatus on tour, once bouncing a kangaroo on one for a promotional stunt. Trampolining became an Olympic gymnastics discipline in 2000, at the Sydney Games, 66 years after that first frame in Iowa.

Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield's rematch in June 1997 was billed as a chance for Tyson to reclaim the heavyweight title he had lost to Holyfield seven months earlier. Tyson complained afterward that Holyfield had repeatedly head-butted him without the referee intervening, and in the third round he responded by biting a chunk out of Holyfield's right ear.

Referee Mills Lane deducted two points and let the fight continue, but Tyson bit the same ear again minutes later, prompting Lane to disqualify him on the spot. Tyson's boxing licence was revoked by the Nevada State Athletic Commission and later reinstated after roughly a year, but the bout remained the defining image of his decline as a fighter.

Cycling already had an international body before 1900, but the International Cycling Association was run largely by the British and was widely resented on the continent. Delegates from France, Belgium, the United States, Switzerland and Italy met in Paris in April 1900 and set up a rival organisation, the Union Cycliste Internationale, deliberately excluding Britain from the founding vote.

The UCI took over sanctioning world championships and, eventually, the sport's biggest races and its governing rulebook. Britain joined only years later once the new body had clearly won out. More than a century on, the UCI still runs from Switzerland and remains the authority behind the Tour de France, the Olympics and every UCI-ranked race on the calendar.

The first World Cup penalty awarded by video review came in the opening match of the 2018 tournament in Russia, when the referee overturned an initial no-call against France's Antoine Griezmann for a foul by Australia. FIFA had approved VAR for competition use only months earlier, and Russia 2018 was its first outing at a men's World Cup.

The system used pitch-side monitors and a review booth in Moscow, and it settled several tight calls that pre-VAR officiating would have missed entirely: shirt-pulls in the box, offside margins measured in centimetres, handballs from deflections. Fans and commentators argued for months over how much it slowed the game down for the sake of getting the call right.

Matthew Webb was a merchant navy captain, not a career swimmer, when he set out from Dover on 24 August 1875 coated in porpoise oil against the cold. A first attempt days earlier had failed against wind and tide, and this one still took almost 22 hours of breaststroke, fighting currents that pushed him well off a straight line.

He landed near Calais to a reception of cheering locals, having covered close to 39 miles of actual swimming to cross a strait only 21 miles wide at its narrowest. No one repeated the feat unaided for 36 years, and Webb died attempting to swim the rapids below Niagara Falls in 1883.

Johnny Weissmuller was 18 and swimming in a salt-water pool in Alameda, California, on 9 July 1922 when he covered 100 metres freestyle in 58.6 seconds, without the benefit of starting blocks or a flip turn. The previous record, 1:00.4, had stood in the name of the Hawaiian swimmer Duke Kahanamoku.

Weissmuller went on to win five Olympic gold medals before leaving the sport for Hollywood, where he played Tarzan in a dozen films through the 1930s and 1940s. His swimming fame is now overshadowed by the film role, though it was the stopwatch, not a studio, that made him a household name first.

No account from 1823 mentions William Webb Ellis picking up the ball and running, and he himself never claimed the feat in a life spent afterward as a clergyman. The story first appeared in print in 1876, four years after his death and more than fifty years after the supposed match, in a letter to the Rugby School magazine from a former pupil recalling something he had been told.

Historians who have examined the surviving evidence treat the tale as invented, yet it stuck: the trophy awarded to the Rugby World Cup winner is named after Webb Ellis, and a plaque at Rugby School still marks the spot where the game he never played is said to have begun.

Barely 4,000 people watched Wilt Chamberlain score 100 points in Hershey, Pennsylvania, on 2 March 1962, because the Philadelphia Warriors had shifted the game there for a bigger arena elsewhere in the state and it drew little local interest. No television cameras covered it, and no footage of the game is known to survive.

Chamberlain made 36 of 63 field goals and, unusually for him, 28 of 32 free throws against the New York Knicks, in a 169-147 Warriors win. His teammates fed him deliberately once the record came into range, and the Knicks stalled by fouling other players to keep the ball from him. No NBA player has since scored more than 81 points in a game.

Walter Clopton Wingfield did not invent hitting a ball over a net, a game with roots stretching back centuries indoors. What he patented in 1874 was a portable kit: poles, netting, rackets and a rulebook for playing the game outdoors on grass, sold in a box for lawn parties.

He called it Sphairistike, from Greek for skill at ball, a name nobody could pronounce and that quickly gave way to lawn tennis. The kit sold well among the Victorian leisured classes, and within a decade it had eclipsed croquet as the fashionable garden pastime that produced Wimbledon.

Winx retired from racing the way she had run for four years: in front. Her final start, the Queen Elizabeth Stakes at Randwick in April 2019, was her 33rd consecutive win, a run without defeat stretching back to 2015 and a record for a top-level horse anywhere in the world.

Jockey Hugh Bowman settled the mare mid-field before sweeping four wide into the straight and drawing clear again, a pattern crowds had watched for years without it ever getting old. The win also gave trainer Chris Waller his 100th Group One victory, and it extended Winx's own Group One tally to 25 before she was retired to stud.

Earlier attempts at a US women's professional basketball league, including one in the late 1970s, had folded within a few seasons for lack of funding and broadcast support. The NBA backed a new attempt in 1996, and the Women's National Basketball Association began play in June 1997 with eight teams tied to existing NBA markets and arenas.

The Houston Comets, led by Cynthia Cooper, won the first championship that August and went on to win the league's first four titles in a row. Unlike the earlier failed leagues, the WNBA's direct NBA financial backing let it survive early low attendance, and it remains the longest-running women's professional sports league in the United States.

Pierre de Coubertin had not wanted women at his Olympics at all, considering it impractical, unaesthetic and incorrect. The 1900 Paris Games let a small number in anyway, mostly through golf and tennis, sports where mixed clubs already existed, and organisers still treated the events as an afterthought rather than part of the official programme they were later recognised as.

Charlotte Cooper, already a Wimbledon champion, won the singles tennis title and then the mixed doubles with Reginald Doherty, becoming the first individual woman to win an Olympic championship. Only around twenty-two women competed among more than nine hundred athletes that year; it took until 2012 for every sport at a Summer Games to include a women's event.

Only five track and field events were open to women at the 1928 Amsterdam Games, after years of resistance from Olympic officials who doubted women could handle distance running at all. Germany's Lina Radke won the inaugural women's 800 metres in a world record of 2 minutes 16.8 seconds, with six of the nine finishers beating the previous mark.

Newspaper reports, later shown to be exaggerated, claimed several runners collapsed at the finish, when in fact one competitor needed help afterward. The uproar those stories caused got the 800 metres pulled from the women's programme entirely, and it did not return to the Olympics until Rome in 1960.

The gymnastics on offer at Amsterdam in 1928 bore little resemblance to the sport now shown at every Games. Women competed only in a team event, performed in matching skirted outfits, with no individual all-around or apparatus finals; those would not arrive for decades.

The Netherlands won the inaugural team title on home ground, a result later shadowed by an unresolved dispute over the eligibility of some competitors' ages. It would be another 20 years before women's gymnastics returned to the Olympic programme, at London in 1948, this time to stay.

Women had been boxing competitively for over a century, but the IOC kept the sport out of the Olympics on grounds ranging from safety to simple reluctance, even after men's boxing had been on the programme since 1904. London 2012 finally added three women's weight divisions, the last new event added to that Games' schedule.

Nicola Adams won the flyweight final on the opening day of women's boxing, beating China's Ren Cancan, and became the first woman to win an Olympic boxing gold medal. The lightweight and middleweight titles followed within the same fortnight, and all three winners came home to attention that had never existed for the sport before.

Archery had already had one turn at the Olympics, appearing sporadically between 1900 and 1920 without standard rules, and was dropped afterwards for lack of one. Delegates from seven countries, France, Czechoslovakia, Sweden, Poland, the United States, Hungary and Italy, met in Lwow in September 1931 to found FITA and fix that.

A single governing body meant a single rulebook, and with it a case for the sport's return to the Games. Archery came back to the Olympic programme in 1972. FITA itself was renamed World Archery in 2011, the name it still carries as the sport's global authority.

The 2019 Cricket World Cup final at Lord's finished tied twice over: England and New Zealand scored 241 apiece after fifty overs each, then tied again in the super over, six balls each side, at 15 runs. Under the rules in force that day, the trophy went to whichever side had hit more boundaries across the whole match, and that was England.

England's total included 26 boundaries to New Zealand's 17, a margin that felt almost arbitrary to decide a world title, and the boundary countback rule was scrapped the following year. Ben Stokes's diving finish in the last over of the innings, where the ball deflected off his bat for four overthrows, remains the match's most argued moment.

Rallying had existed for decades before 1973, but as a scattered set of national events with no shared championship. The FIA created a single World Rally Championship for manufacturers that year, folding in events already famous in their own right, including the Monte Carlo Rally, the Safari Rally and the RAC Rally.

Thirteen rounds counted toward the inaugural title, and Alpine-Renault won it, its lightweight A110 suited to the mix of tarmac and gravel stages. A drivers' championship was not added until 1979; before that, only the manufacturers' crown existed, which is why 1973 is remembered as a title for a factory rather than a driver.

For the first thirteen recorded Olympiads the only event was a footrace. In 708 BCE the programme at Olympia grew to include wrestling and the pentathlon, a single combined contest of running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling rather than five separate medals. The winner of the pentathlon's wrestling round, contested last, was the overall victor if the scoring still stood in his favour.

The pentathlon was designed to reward the complete athlete rather than a specialist sprinter, and ancient writers treated its winners as the Games' best all-round competitors. Wrestling on its own also became one of the longest-running Olympic events, surviving in recognisable form for over a thousand years. Its introduction marked the point where Olympia stopped being a running festival and became a multi-sport games.

Minamoto no Yoritomo did not invent mounted archery, which had existed in Japan for centuries, but as the first shogun he formalised yabusame at Tsurugaoka Hachimangu as a rite meant to keep his samurai sharp once the fighting that won him power had stopped. Riders gallop past three fixed targets, drawing and loosing in the seconds each one is in range.

The bow is asymmetric, gripped below its centre so a mounted archer can clear the horse's neck, and the archer rides with both hands off the reins at the moment of the shot, steering by knee pressure alone. The ritual is still performed at the same shrine, dressed in the hunting costume of Yoritomo's own retainers.

Emil Zatopek had never raced a marathon before the one he won. At the 1952 Helsinki Olympics he took the 10,000 metres first, then the 5,000 metres days later despite not being the favourite in either, and finished by entering the marathon almost as an experiment, running beside Jim Peters, the world's fastest marathoner, until Peters dropped away and Zatopek pulled clear to win that too.

No athlete before or since has won all three distance events at a single Olympics; even Zatopek's own wife, javelin thrower Dana Zatopkova, won gold at the same Games. His training, built around punishing interval repeats that other runners considered close to reckless, became the template distance coaches still borrow from.
